issues.title: Nothing checks that a build leaves the worktree clean, so generated-file drift lands silently
issues.body:
Split out of #260, which fixes the current instance and explicitly declines to add this gate: "That is a new gate rather than a fix, so it belongs to whoever owns the CI surface — noting it here rather than assuming it." Filing it so the suggestion outlives that issue.

## What is missing

`apps/web/next-env.d.ts` is a tracked generated file. Next regenerates it on every `next build` and every `tsc`. When a Next upgrade changes what it generates, the committed copy goes stale and every build from then on dirties the worktree — for everyone, indefinitely, until somebody notices and commits the new output.

That is #260, introduced by #225 (`next` 16.2.12 -> 16.3.0) and only found weeks later by someone building `main` locally.

**Nothing failed in between.** `Web App CI` runs `npm run ci:web` -> lint, typecheck, test, build, and the job ends. The regenerated file is discarded with the runner. There is no step comparing the worktree against what the build produced, so the drift is invisible to CI by construction.

## The check

One step after the build, in the job that already runs it:

```yaml
- name: Build must leave the worktree clean
  run: git diff --exit-code
```

Roughly free — no new build, no new install, one `git diff` on a tree that is already there.

## What makes this worth more than the one file it would have caught

`next-env.d.ts` is the instance, not the class. Any tracked file that a build or codegen step rewrites has the same shape: Prisma client output, a generated type, a lockfile touched by an install. The failure mode is identical each time — CI green, every local `git status` dirty, and the cost paid by whoever next tries to read their own diff.

It also lands on this repository's own workflow. `AGENTS.md` step 5 asks for the complete diff including unstaged files to be inspected, and step 10 treats any changed worktree content as a state change that can re-arm code review. A file that reliably appears there costs a decision on every single change, and trains people to skim past exactly the output those steps exist to make them read.

## Decide before implementing

This changes what CI does for every contributor, so it is worth saying out loud rather than adding quietly:

- **A false positive blocks the merge queue.** If any build step legitimately writes into the worktree on some machine or some run, this turns that into a hard failure. Whether anything currently does is not established — worth checking `prisma generate` and the Docker build path before turning it on.
- **Which job.** `Web App CI` is the narrow answer and catches the known case. A repo-wide check would catch the chat and script surfaces too, at the cost of a step in more jobs.
- **`git diff --exit-code` vs `git status --porcelain`.** The first ignores untracked files; the second catches a build that writes a *new* untracked file, which is arguably also drift and arguably just build output that belongs in `.gitignore`.

## How it was found

#260 was reproduced twice while working #302 and #305 — every `tsc --noEmit` and every `next build` during that change put `next-env.d.ts` back in `git status`, and it had to be reverted by hand before each commit so it stayed out of two unrelated diffs. That is the recurring cost this gate would remove, and the reason it seems worth more than the single line it checks.
issues.display_title: Nothing checks that a build leaves the worktree clean, so generated-file drift lands silently

issues.title: /login and /signup are navigational dead ends: no header, no links, not even to each other
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` while rendering PR #300 (a `next` 16.3.0 -> 16.3.1 bump). Pre-existing, and provably so — the same review found zero differing pixels between the two builds across 145.5M pixels compared.

## Measured

Against the production build on both pages, at every viewport:

```
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3201/login  | grep -o '<a [^>]*href=' | wc -l
0
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3201/signup | grep -o '<a [^>]*href=' | wc -l
0
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3201/login  | grep -o '<header' | wc -l
0
```

Zero anchors and no `<header>` on either page. The full tab order on `/login` is:

```
email > password > Sign in > Open chat
```

So there is no link from Sign In to Sign Up, none the other way, and no route back into the site except the browser's Back button. The chat launcher is the only other interactive element on the page.

## Why it matters

Sign-in and sign-up are the two pages a visitor is most likely to arrive at from outside the site, and they are the two with no way onward. A visitor who lands on `/login` without an account has no path to registration, which is the one thing that page should always offer.

It also breaks the pattern every other page follows: `/`, `/about`, `/faq` and `/contact` all render the header with its navigation.

## Suggested fix

The cross-link is the substantive half — "Don't have an account? Sign up" on `/login` and its inverse on `/signup`. Whether these pages should also render the full header is a separate call: a deliberately stripped auth page is a legitimate design, but a dead end is not, and today's state is not obviously the former rather than an oversight.

## Not established

Whether the missing header is deliberate. Nothing in the components says either way, and there is no comment recording a decision — which is itself worth fixing, since the next person cannot tell an intentional stripped-down auth page from a page that never got one.

## Why it was not fixed at the time

Found during a dependency-bump review whose diff is two lines of `package.json`. It needs a small design decision about the header, so it does not belong inside that bump.
issues.display_title: /login and /signup are navigational dead ends: no header, no links, not even to each other

issues.title: The journeys' no-retry policy is guarded by a regex over the config text, not the resolved value
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` during #283, which added a vitest-side flake guard that reads the resolved value from the runner. That made the journey side the weaker half of the pair.

## What is wrong

`tests/scripts/test_e2e_journey_wiring.py::test_retries_are_not_enabled` asserts on the *text* of `apps/web/playwright.config.ts`:

```python
config = read("apps/web/playwright.config.ts")
self.assertRegex(config, re.compile(r"retries:\s*0"))
```

That is a declaration read, not a measurement. It passes while retries are on if `retries: 0` appears anywhere in the file — in a comment, in a dead object literal, in a `projects[]` entry that is not the live one — and the live value is `2`. It is the shape the root `AGENTS.md` *Code Review Rules* tell reviewers to reject: "Require guards to measure effective behavior, not a nearby declaration."

Nothing is wrong with the current value. `playwright.config.ts` does state `retries: 0` unconditionally today, with no `process.env.CI ? 2 : 0`. This is about what the guard would notice if that changed.

## What the equivalent measurement looks like

Playwright exposes the resolved value to a spec through `testInfo.project.retries`, so a journey can assert what the runner will actually do, the way `apps/web/src/test/runner-budget.test.ts` now does for vitest via `task.timeout` and `task.retry`:

```ts
test('the journeys do not retry', ({}, testInfo) => {
  expect(testInfo.project.retries).toBe(0)
})
```

Two things to weigh before doing that:

- A journey spec needs the composed stack to run, so this moves a check that currently costs milliseconds in `make test-scripts` into a suite that costs minutes and needs docker. A spec that asserts only on `testInfo` touches no page, but it still runs inside the run that needs the stack.
- The python guard also runs on machines that never build a stack, which is part of why it is where it is.

So the options are: replace the regex with a journey assertion, keep both (cheap declaration check plus effective check), or leave it and accept that the journey policy is guarded more weakly than the unit one. Worth a deliberate choice rather than the current implicit one.

## Also worth noting

`timeout: 30_000` and `expect: { timeout: 10_000 }` in the same file are guarded by nothing at all. If a runner-read check gets added, those are the same `testInfo.project`/`testInfo.timeout` read and cost nothing extra.
issues.display_title: The journeys' no-retry policy is guarded by a regex over the config text, not the resolved value

issues.title: detect_changed_surfaces misreads C-quoted paths, so a filename with a space classifies as unknown
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` during #253, and it lands on the same flag that change was tightening.

## Measured

`changed_files_from_range` and `changed_files_from_worktree` in `scripts/detect_changed_surfaces.py` take git's path output literally. Git C-quotes any path containing a space or a non-ASCII byte, so those paths arrive wrapped in quotes and with escapes intact. Reproduced in a scratch repository:

```
$ git status --porcelain
 M "apps/web/a b.ts"
 M "apps/web/na\303\257ve.ts"
```

Both strings reach `matches_any` with the quoting attached. `apps/web/**` does not match `"apps/web/a b.ts"`, so an ordinary tracked source file classifies as `unknown`.

## Why it matters more than it looks

Routing fails in the safe direction — `unknown` forces the full runtime recommendation, so nothing is under-gated and no check is skipped. That is why it has never been visible.

The cost is to the flag rather than to the gate. `unknown` is supposed to mean "no pattern claims this path", and #253 has just narrowed it for exactly that reason: every classified file sheltering under the fallback makes the flag harder to tighten later without silently reclassifying whatever else was hiding there. A renamed component with a space in its filename reads, to that flag, as an unclassified path.

It also degrades the local loop more than CI. `make quick-ci-changed` uses the worktree path, so a developer working on such a file gets the full runtime target list rather than the web one, with no indication why.

## Fix

Pass `git -c core.quotePath=false` so non-ASCII comes through literally, and unquote the `"..."` form for the cases that remain (a literal quote, backslash, newline or tab in a filename still gets quoted regardless of `quotePath`).

`--porcelain=v1` documents the quoting rule; `-z` with NUL separators is the other standard answer and avoids the unquoting entirely, at the cost of changing how both readers split their output.

## Worth knowing when fixing

Both readers need it, not just one. `changed_files_from_range` feeds CI through `--base`/`--head`, and `changed_files_from_worktree` feeds `make quick-ci-changed`; the two take different git commands and only the second was exercised in the reproduction above.

A guard belongs with it — `tests/scripts/test_detect_changed_surfaces.py` already patches `run_git` for `test_changed_files_from_range_includes_deletions`, so a case returning a C-quoted path fits the existing shape.
issues.display_title: detect_changed_surfaces misreads C-quoted paths, so a filename with a space classifies as unknown

issues.title: The docker-compose runtime rationale has been false since #124, in the comment and its test
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` during #253, which had copied the stale sentence into a new comment before it was caught.

## The claim, in two places

`scripts/detect_changed_surfaces.py`, on the `docker-compose.yml` entry in `RUNTIME_PATTERNS`:

> Compose is web+chat, but the guard that protects its startup ordering lives in tests/scripts. Without this, a change dropping the healthcheck would never run that guard.

and `tests/scripts/test_detect_changed_surfaces.py`, in `test_compose_changes_are_runtime`:

> docker-compose.yml already matched web and chat, so it never reached the unknown fallback. Without an explicit runtime pattern, a compose-only change would skip test-scripts and the startup-ordering guard that protects it.

Both say the runtime classification is what makes `test-scripts` run for a compose change. It is not, and has not been since the day after they were written.

## Measured

`test-scripts` runs for *every* non-empty change, whatever its surface:

```python
# scripts/detect_changed_surfaces.py, the non-runtime branch
if not flags["none"]:
    ordered.append("test-scripts")
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml, the script-tests job
if: ${{ github.event_name != 'push' && needs.changes.outputs.none != 'true' }}
```

Confirmed against a surface that is not runtime at all:

```
$ classify(['README.md'])            -> {'docs': True}
$ recommended_targets(...)           -> ['test-scripts', 'docs-check']
```

So a docs-only change already runs the guardrail suite. Removing `docker-compose.yml` from `RUNTIME_PATTERNS` would not stop the startup-ordering guard running — compose already matches `WEB_PATTERNS` and `CHAT_PATTERNS`, so it never reached the `unknown` fallback either, which the test's own docstring says.

## How it went stale

`d8fd6ff` (#111) added the comment when it was true. `eadda07` (#124) made `test-scripts` run for every non-empty change the next day, which invalidated it. Neither the comment nor the docstring was revisited.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than leaving

It is load-bearing prose in the file that decides what CI runs, and it reads as audited. #253 is the demonstration: writing a new entry in the same tuple, I copied the reasoning from the entry above and recorded a justification that had been false for two weeks. `code-review` caught it there. The original is still sitting in the file for the next person to copy.

`test_compose_changes_are_runtime`'s `assertIn("test-scripts", ...)` also passes with or without the compose entry, so the assertion does not measure what its docstring claims.

## Suggested fix

Correct both to the reason that does hold — compose is web and chat, and the entry makes that classification explicit rather than leaving it to two surface patterns — or, if the entry turns out to buy nothing at all now, say so and consider whether it should stay.
issues.display_title: The docker-compose runtime rationale has been false since #124, in the comment and its test

issues.title: test_agent_definitions only guards agent names below one heading, so names elsewhere in AGENTS.md can go stale
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` while reviewing the AGENTS.md change that adds *Unrelated findings become issues*. Same shape as #100, lower severity, so filing rather than widening a documentation change.

## What is unguarded

`tests/scripts/test_agent_definitions.py` exists so AGENTS.md cannot claim a sub-agent that does not exist. But `agent_names_claimed_by_docs()` splits the file at the `### Sub-agents this workflow depends on` heading and only scans below it.

The new section names all three agents above that heading:

```
`ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` read more of the repository than the
change touches.
```

Rename or remove an agent and that line goes stale with the test green.

## Why it is minor

The guarded section would fail first on the same rename, so the failure is loud and the stale line gets found while fixing it. And the claim above the heading is only a *name*, not a capability — the class of thing #100 was filed about (prose asserting behaviour nothing enforces) is not what is unguarded here.

Worth fixing when the file is next touched rather than on its own.

## Options

1. Scan the whole file for agent-name references instead of the region below one heading. Straightforward, but it widens what the test treats as a claim — mentions in prose, examples and troubleshooting all become assertions.
2. Keep the region split and add a narrower whole-file check for backticked names matching a known agent-name shape.

(1) is probably right if the false-positive rate turns out to be low; worth counting the matches across the current file before deciding.
issues.display_title: test_agent_definitions only guards agent names below one heading, so names elsewhere in AGENTS.md can go stale

issues.title: Nothing tells ui-review that keyboard journeys need a production build
issues.body:
Found while fixing #277, which turned out to narrow this problem rather than end it.

## The measurement

Next's dev overlay renders a focusable element positioned after the chat widget in the document. With the panel open at 1440x900, tabbing forward from the message input:

```
clean dev server                  after one logged error
1. Send message      dialog=1     1. Send message              dialog=1
2. Close chat        dialog=1     2. Close chat                dialog=1
3. BODY              dialog=1     3. Open issues overlay       dialog=0  <- shadow DOM
4. #name             dialog=0     4. Collapse issues badge     dialog=0
                                  5. BODY
```

The left column is what a production build does. The right column is dev with an error logged, and the panel closes a keystroke early because the extra stop is inside the page and fires `focusin`.

`devIndicators: false` (#277) removes the *idle* badge, which is why the left column is now the clean-state behaviour. It does not remove the *issues* badge, and it should not — that badge is how errors surface.

The catch is how easily this application reaches the right-hand column. `chat.tsx`'s `settleWithError` calls `console.error("Chat request failed:", error)`, so a single chat send against a stack with no chat service produces it. That is the ordinary local configuration.

At 390x844 the same badge covers the input's left third: `elementFromPoint` at 5%, 15% and 30% of the input's width returns `NEXTJS-PORTAL`, and the placeholder reads "...roduct...".

## What needs saying, and where

`ui-review` currently has no instruction about which stack a keyboard journey needs. Its *Rendering the application* section covers whether a browser is reachable and which tool drives it, and #279 added what to do when the MCP server fails — but nothing says that tab order, focus-out behaviour and anything else the dev overlay participates in must be measured against a production build to mean anything.

This matters more since #282, which made the chat panel reachable under `next dev` at all. Before it, chat journeys were unrunnable locally without docker and the question could not arise.

`chat.tsx` is the component most exposed: its focus-out close, its Tab-forward-leaves-the-page reasoning, and its trap are all sensitive to what sits after the widget in the document. A review that measures those on a dev server is measuring the dev server.

## Options

1. A sentence in `.claude/agents/ui-review.md` naming the classes of finding that need a production build, with tab order and focus-out the examples.
2. The same in root `AGENTS.md` step 6, which already discusses when a stack is needed.
3. Both, if the runbook states the requirement and the agent states the mechanic.

Whichever, it should be specific about the trigger rather than general — "use production for keyboard journeys" invites the reply that dev looked fine, which it does until something logs an error.
issues.display_title: Nothing tells ui-review that keyboard journeys need a production build

issues.title: On the phone sheet, Send appears exactly where the launcher was tapped
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` at 390x844 while reviewing #277.

## Measured

On the phone sheet, the launcher and the send button occupy the same origin:

- launcher, before opening: `{x: 334, y: 788, w: 40, h: 40}`
- `Send message`, after opening: `{x: 334, y: 788, w: 44, h: 44}`

The launcher is unmounted while the sheet is open — `!(isCompact && showChat)` — so these two never coexist. The problem is that the second appears exactly where the first was, under a pointer that has not moved. It is measurable: after opening by tap, Send reports its hover fill, sky-800 `lab(35.16 -9.58 -34.41)`, rather than the resting sky-700 `lab(41.60 -9.11 -42.56)` it shows at desktop where the pointer is elsewhere.

So the control the user just pressed is replaced, under their finger, by a different control.

## Why it is worth recording

`chat.tsx` already treats this hazard as handled. The comment on the sheet's close button (around lines 526-538) explains that dismissal moved into the header partly to "un-crowd the bottom right", describing the old arrangement as "two icon-only controls of near-identical size in one column, where a mis-tap discards the message being composed".

That fix addressed the launcher-versus-close collision. The launcher-versus-send collision is the same shape and survived it, at the same coordinates.

Harm today is small: a double tap sends an empty message, and #197 records that an empty send is a no-op. It stops being small if #197 is fixed such that the button does something on an empty field, or once there is text in the input — then a stray second tap sends a half-composed message.

## Not established

Whether the same collision exists at other phone widths or only where the launcher's `mr-4 mb-4` and the input row's padding happen to coincide. Only 390x844 was measured. Worth checking 360 and 430 before choosing a fix, since the remedy differs if the overlap is coincidental at one width rather than structural.
issues.display_title: On the phone sheet, Send appears exactly where the launcher was tapped

issues.title: Should a focus landing on document.body close the chat panel?
issues.body:
Split out of #228. That issue's root cause turned out to be Next's dev-server cross-origin gate rather than anything in `chat.tsx` (see the comment there for the measurement), so its closing question was never actually exercised by the repro and is still open on its own merits.

## The question

`apps/web/src/components/chat.tsx:217-230` closes the panel whenever focus moves outside the widget:

```ts
const onFocusIn = (event: FocusEvent) => {
  const target = event.target as Node | null
  if (target && widgetRef.current?.contains(target)) return
  closedByFocusOut.current = true
  setShowChat(false)
}
```

Should a focus landing on `document.body` close the panel at all?

`relatedTarget === null`, or a `body` target, is the browser losing focus rather than the user moving it somewhere. That is the same distinction the comment block above the effect already draws for the address bar — it explains at length why the effect is backwards-only, because Tab forward off the last control leaves the page entirely and dismissing the panel for that would be closing it for something that is not a page interaction.

Focus falling to `body` is arguably the same class of event: no control gained focus, so no control can be obscured by the panel, and 2.4.11 — the criterion the effect exists to satisfy — is about the focused control.

## Why it is not obviously safe to change

The effect is only active at `lg` and up (`if (!showChat || isCompact) return`), where the surrounding page is not `inert`. Focus can reach `body` there by routes that are genuine user actions, and the comment already notes one the effect deliberately does not handle: clicking bare page fires no `focusin` at all, so the panel stays up — recorded as #187.

So the change would be narrow: ignore `focusin` whose target is `document.body` (or whose `relatedTarget` is null), and leave every other outside target closing the panel as it does now.

## What to check when picking this up

- Which real interactions actually land focus on `body` at `lg` and up. This needs measuring rather than reasoning about; the answer decides whether the change is worth making.
- `chat.test.tsx` covers the focus-out close path — see the effect's own comment for which assertions cover which branches, and which branches nothing covers.
- Whether ignoring `body` reopens the WCAG 3.2.1 concern the focus-return effect at `chat.tsx:271` was written for.

Not urgent, and not blocking anything.
issues.display_title: Should a focus landing on document.body close the chat panel?

issues.title: An invalid field is pixel-identical to a focused valid one, and announces nothing
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #196. ## Measured Clicking **Send Message** on `/contact` with the fields empty: - `#name` matches `:invalid`, but its computed ring is `sky-700` and its outline is `sky-700 solid 2px` — **pixel-identical to a normally focused, perfectly valid field**. Nothing distinguishes "this is wrong" from "you are here". - Across all ten fields on `/login`, `/signup` and `/contact`: `aria-invalid` is `null` and `aria-describedby` is `null`. - The error `

` carries no `role="alert"` and no `aria-live`, so a screen-reader user is told nothing when it appears. So the error state is invisible to someone who cannot see, and ambiguous to someone who can. ## Why now Pre-existing on every count. It is filed now because #196 is the moment these fields' visual language got centralised: with `FIELD_BOUNDARY` in `apps/web/src/lib/field-classes.ts`, an `aria-[invalid=true]:ring-red-600` is a one-line addition rather than ten edits in three files. Note the ARIA half is the larger half and the constant cannot help with it — `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` have to be wired per field, and the error element needs a live region. A red ring alone would fix the ambiguity for sighted users and leave the announcement gap exactly where it is. Related: #216 (the same ring vanishes entirely in forced-colors, so a colour-only error state would too), #217 (placeholder contrast on the same fields). ## Why it was not fixed in #196 #196's scope is the resting boundary failing 1.4.11. An error state is new behaviour, needs a decision about wording and announcement, and touches the form logic rather than its styling.
issues.display_title: An invalid field is pixel-identical to a focused valid one, and announces nothing

issues.title: Contact form placeholders are 2.23:1 — weaker than the box they sit in
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #196.

## Measured

Rendered on `/contact #name` at 1440x900:

| | measured |
|---|---|
| darkest placeholder glyph | rgb(153,161,175) on field surface rgb(238,237,236) = **2.23:1** |
| the field's boundary, after #196 | **4.13:1** |

WCAG 2.2 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), Level AA, asks 4.5:1 of text. The border is now **1.9x the contrast of the hint text inside it**, which is a strange thing to ship: the box shouts and its content whispers.

`/contact` is the only one of the three forms with placeholders. `/login` and `/signup` have none.

## It also undercuts what #196 set out to do

#196's premise was that eleven fields should not style themselves independently. The ring is now identical across all eleven; the placeholder is not:

| | placeholder |
|---|---|
| chat panel input | `placeholder:text-zinc-500 placeholder:opacity-100` — 4.83:1 on white |
| the ten page fields | `placeholder:text-gray-400` — 2.60:1 on white, 2.23:1 on the contact card |

The user chose "match the chat panel exactly" for the boundary. This is the part that still does not match.

## Why it was not fixed in #196

Different criterion. #196 is 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, about a control's *boundary*; this is 1.4.3, about *text*. The constant is called `FIELD_BOUNDARY` and a placeholder is not a boundary, so folding it in would either mis-name the constant or quietly widen what it owns.

Worth deciding together with that naming: if the constant is to carry placeholder colour, disabled styling and invalid styling (see #217), it should be `FIELD_CLASSES` and say so.
issues.display_title: Contact form placeholders are 2.23:1 — weaker than the box they sit in

issues.title: Contact page heading and subheading fall below WCAG AA against the busiest parts of the background
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` on `perf/optimise-background-images` (#158). **Pre-existing and identical before and after that change** — the re-encode moves contrast by at most 0.16 ratio points — so it is not a regression, but it is the one real contrast problem on a page that PR touches.

## Measured

Worst-pixel ratio against the actual rendered background, with glyphs hidden and the background sampled underneath:

| element | required | phone | tablet | desktop | mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "Get in Touch" (large text) | 3.0 | 4.89 | 3.22 | **2.87** | 7.3–9.6 |
| "Ready for your next adventure?" (20px/400) | 4.5 | **2.94** | **2.53** | **3.43** | 7.3–8.0 |

`apps/web/src/app/contact/page.tsx`. The subheading is below AA at all three viewports; the heading at desktop.

## Why the mean is misleading here

The mean ratio is comfortable everywhere — 7.3 and up. Text over a photograph is not judged against the mean: it is judged against the brightest region it actually overlaps, because that is where the glyphs disappear. The existing `bg-gray-900/40` wash and 2px backdrop blur lift the average without flattening the highlights.

`/contact/thanks` is fine — 14.6 and 6.2 — because its copy sits on an opaque card rather than directly on the image.

## Options

1. **Deepen the wash behind the heading block specifically** — a local gradient or a second scrim over just that region, leaving the rest of the image as it is.
2. **Give the heading and subheading a text shadow or a local scrim.** The heading already has `drop-shadow-md` and the subheading `drop-shadow-xs`; those are shadows for depth, not for contrast, and are too soft to carry it.
3. **Raise the global wash** past 40%. Simplest, and costs the image most.

(1) or (2) keeps the photograph readable while fixing the text.

## Worth knowing

Nothing in the suite measures this. The rendered contrast check that produced these numbers samples the composited background under each text box — that is not something `ui-review` can do on every run without being asked, and there is no automated equivalent in the repo.
issues.display_title: Contact page heading and subheading fall below WCAG AA against the busiest parts of the background

issues.title: The chat launcher overlaps the submit button on /contact at phone width
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` at 390x844 on `/contact`, while it was being used to exercise an unrelated change.

## Measured

At 390x844 on `/contact`:

- chat launcher: x 334-374, y 788-828
- `Send Message` button: x 48-342, y 796-848

They overlap. `document.elementFromPoint` at 99% of the submit button's width returns the launcher, not the button — so roughly the last 8px of the page's primary action is not the primary action. A tap there opens the chat instead of submitting the form.

Separately, the submit button's bottom edge is at y=848 against a 844px viewport, so the primary action is not fully on screen without scrolling.

## Why this is worth more than the 8px

The launcher is `fixed bottom-0 right-0` with `mr-4 mb-4` below `sm`, so it sits over whatever the page puts in its bottom-right corner, on every page. `/contact` is the case where what it lands on is a submit button, but the general problem is that no page's layout reserves space for it.

That makes it a near relative of #187 — a chat surface covering page content that the page cannot scroll clear — but at phone width and against a form control rather than product links, and caused by the launcher rather than the panel.

The mis-tap is also the failure mode `chat.tsx` already worries about one control over: the comment on the sheet's close button (around lines 526-538) explains that the launcher used to float over the sheet 20px below the send button, and calls that "two icon-only controls of near-identical size in one column, where a mis-tap discards the message being composed". The same reasoning applies to a launcher sitting on a form's submit.

## Options

1. Bottom padding on `main` at phone widths, sized to clear the launcher. Fixes every page at once, costs vertical space on all of them.
2. Offset the launcher on pages whose primary action is bottom-right. Targeted, but needs per-page knowledge and will be forgotten by the next page that has one.
3. Leave the overlap and only fix the fold, which addresses the smaller half.

Option 1 is the one that does not depend on remembering.

## Not established

Whether other pages have a bottom-right control under the launcher — only `/contact` was measured. Worth sweeping before choosing, because the answer decides between options 1 and 2.
issues.display_title: The chat launcher overlaps the submit button on /contact at phone width

issues.title: Root-level test files in apps/web are never type-checked
issues.body:
Found by `verifier` during #228, when asked to confirm that the type-check step was happy with a newly added root-level test. It is happy with it in the sense that it never opens it.

## What is not covered

`apps/web/tsconfig.json`'s `include` is `next-env.d.ts`, `src/**/*.ts(x)`, `prisma/**/*.ts` and the generated `.next` types. Root-level files are in none of those, so `make typecheck` never sees:

- `apps/web/next.config.test.ts` (pre-existing)
- `apps/web/next-dev-origins.test.ts` (added in #228)

Confirmed rather than inferred:

```
$ ./node_modules/.bin/tsc --noEmit --listFilesOnly | grep -i "next-dev-origins\|next.config.test"
(no matches)
```

`vitest.config.ts` has no `typecheck` block either, so vitest's esbuild transform strips the types without checking them. Net effect: these files are exercised at runtime by vitest and statically checked by nothing in the merge gate.

## Why it is worth closing

The repository already treats "a test file that nothing type-checks" as a defect worth a guard, one category over. `playwright.config.ts` sets an explicit `testMatch` so that the set of journey files is a single fact, and `tests/scripts/test_e2e_journey_wiring.py` asserts every file it collects is type-checked — written because each un-matched extension was "a journey that ran with nothing type-checking it".

Root-level unit tests are the same hole in a different wall, and there is no equivalent guard.

## Worth knowing before fixing

Adding root-level `*.test.ts` to `include` is the obvious move, but check what it surfaces first — neither file has ever been type-checked, so both may have errors that have simply never been reported.

For `next-dev-origins.test.ts` specifically, type-checking buys less than it looks: the module it reaches for, `next/dist/server/lib/router-utils/block-cross-site-dev.js`, is untyped JavaScript, so `blockCrossSiteDEV` types as `any` however the config is set. Its runtime assertions are what catch a signature change there. The rest of the file would benefit normally.

The other half of the fix is a guard, so this cannot silently regress the way the journey wiring did.
issues.display_title: Root-level test files in apps/web are never type-checked

issues.title: next dev appends a doubled, non-existent .next/dev/dev include to tsconfig.json
issues.body:
Found while fixing #228, which needed a guard that starts a dev server.

**Re-scoped.** This issue originally covered three files. Two of them were already tracked and the content has been moved:

- `apps/web/next-env.d.ts` churn — belongs to #260, where the dev-vs-build conflict is now recorded.
- `apps/web/AGENTS.md` — was #265, fixed by #282 via `agentRules: false`.

What remains here is the part that is nobody else's issue.

## What happens

Once a `next dev` server has served a page, it appends an `include` entry to the tracked `apps/web/tsconfig.json`:

```diff
     ".next/dev/types/**/*.ts",
+    ".next/dev/dev/types/**/*.ts"
```

`.next/dev/dev/` is not a directory that exists and never will be. `distDir` is already `.next/dev`, and `dev/types/**/*.ts` is joined onto it a second time.

The committed `tsconfig.json` already carries both `.next/types/**/*.ts` and `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts`, so this accumulation has happened before and been committed at least once. Each doubled variant is a new entry rather than a replacement, so it grows.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than tolerating

The entry is inert — it matches nothing, so it changes what `tsc` compiles not at all. The problem is where it is inert: `include` is the file that decides what `make typecheck` covers. An entry nobody can account for, in the list that defines type-check scope, is the kind of thing that gets copied or "corrected" later by someone assuming it was deliberate.

It also means `git status` is dirty after a dev session in a *second* file beyond the one #260 tracks, and this one is genuinely hand-maintained — unlike `next-env.d.ts`, `tsconfig.json` cannot simply be ignored.

## Worth checking when picking this up

- Whether this is a Next bug worth reporting upstream. The doubling looks like a plain path-join error rather than a decision.
- Whether the two pre-existing entries, `.next/types/**/*.ts` and `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts`, are both still needed, or whether one of them is the fossil of an earlier round of the same accumulation.
issues.display_title: next dev appends a doubled, non-existent .next/dev/dev include to tsconfig.json

issues.title: Chat card at 1024 reads as an untitled centred dialog, and header buttons are 36x36 against Send's 44x44
issues.body:
Two presentation findings from the rendered reviews during #183. Neither is a conformance failure; both are polish at the card widths.

## 1. 1024 is the weakest width of the six

Measured at 1024×800 with the panel open: card is 650×688 at x=326–976, covering **54.6%** of the viewport, leaving a 326px sliver of page on the left and 48px on the right, and bisecting the header's Sign Up button.

It has no heading — `isCompact` is false, so the `<h2>` added in #129 is not rendered.

#183 moved the modal boundary to `lg` on the argument that "a card is only a card if the page is still there around it" (70–75% coverage at 640–834 was not). At 1024 that argument is weakest on its own terms: 54.6% does not read as a corner card, it reads as a centred dialog missing its backdrop, and it is untitled.

Options: render the title at all widths; cap the card's height so it is genuinely a corner; or accept that 1024 is the awkward end of a range that is fine by 1280.

## 2. Icon button sizes are inconsistent within the panel

Measured at 390, 834 and 1440, unchanged across them:

| control | size |
|---|---|
| Send message | 44×44 |
| launcher | 40×40 |
| Clear conversation | 36×36 |
| Close chat (sheet header) | 36×36 |

All clear WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum, AA, 24×24) comfortably. 36×36 misses 2.5.5 (AAA, 44×44). The real complaint is that three adjacent controls in one panel are three different sizes.

## Not included

The forward-Tab behaviour at `lg`+ — Tab off the last widget control puts focus on `<body>` with the panel still open, and it closes on the next keystroke — is deliberate and documented in `chat.tsx`. In a real browser that stop is the browser's own chrome, and dismissing the panel while the user is in the address bar would be wrong.
issues.display_title: Chat card at 1024 reads as an untitled centred dialog, and header buttons are 36x36 against Send's 44x44

issues.title: At tablet width the category grid's priority cutoff splits a visible row, so adjacent cards arrive 2.7s apart
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` on `perf/prioritise-lcp-images` (#169). A known, measured consequence of the cutoff that PR chose, filed rather than fixed because the alternatives are worse on the numbers.

## What it looks like

`priority={i < 3}` preloads the first three cards. At **834×1112** the grid is two columns, so cards 3 and 4 sit side by side with **251px of each above the fold** — and card 3 is index 2 (eager) while card 4 is index 3 (lazy).

Median load completion over three throttled runs (1.6 Mbps / 150 ms RTT / 4× CPU):

```
card 3 (eager)  1295 ms
card 4 (lazy)   3980 ms
```

A **2.7-second gap between two adjacent, equally visible cards in the same row.** The rendered filmstrip at 2200 ms shows three tents painted and a bare grey box beside the third.

At 1440 the equivalent band is cards 4–6 with 63px visible, and they are uniformly late, which reads as "there is more below" rather than as something broken. At 390 there is no artifact — nothing below card 1 is on screen.

## Why #169 shipped it anyway

`priority` cannot vary by viewport, so one cutoff serves all three layouts. Measured LCP by cutoff, median of 7:

| width | n=0 | n=1 | n=2 | **n=3** | n=6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 390 | 1540 | **736** | 744 | 748 | 840 |
| 834 | 2380 | **1404** | 1480 | 1488 | 1588 |
| 1440 | 2836 | 2972 | 1816 | **1788** | 1900 |

Summed regret against the best value at each width: n=1 costs 1184 ms, n=2 costs 112, **n=3 costs 96**, n=6 costs 400. So 3 is the best available single number, and 6 — which would cover the visible rows at 1440 — is worse everywhere.

Note n=1 is *worse than doing nothing* at 1440.

## Options

1. **Accept it.** The artifact is at one breakpoint band, it is a delay rather than a defect, and CLS is 0.0000 throughout because the `aspect-square` wrapper reserves the box. This is where #169 left it.
2. **A hand-rolled responsive preload.** `<link rel="preload" as="image" media="...">` can vary by viewport where `priority` cannot. Measured ceiling on the gain: **84 ms at 834 and 12 ms at 390**. Real machinery for very little.
3. **Cut at 4.** Untested. It would pair cards 3 and 4 correctly at 834 and cost phones a third off-screen preload; the n=6 row suggests the cost curve is already rising.

(1) unless someone finds the tablet band jarring in practice.

## Worth knowing

`next/image`'s `priority` sets no `fetchpriority` in Next 16.2 — it only flips `loading` and emits a preload link. So preloaded cards compete with the LCP element on equal terms, which is the mechanism behind both the n=1 regression and this artifact.
issues.display_title: At tablet width the category grid's priority cutoff splits a visible row, so adjacent cards arrive 2.7s apart

issues.title: The header avatar is a raw , so react-dom preloads it on every signed-in page
issues.body: Raised twice by `code-review` while reviewing #230 and #263, and filed now rather than a third time. ## What it is `apps/web/src/components/header.tsx:47` renders the signed-in user's avatar as a plain ``: ```jsx ``` Three consequences, in increasing order of interest: 1. **Unoptimised bytes from an external origin.** Whatever the provider returns is what ships — no resizing to the 32px box it is displayed in, no format negotiation, no `sizes`. 2. **It is not lazy**, so react-dom emits a `` for it. That happens on **every page a signed-in user loads**, including the two listing surfaces whose preloads are tuned against largest-contentful-paint. It competes with them on equal terms. 3. **It distorts any test that counts preloads.** `e2e/image-delivery.spec.ts` already scopes its preload assertions to `/_next/image` for exactly this reason, and the new journey in `e2e/image-deferral.spec.ts` had to do the same. Both suites run signed out, so the avatar is absent today — which means an unscoped count would pass for the right reason now and fail with a false message the day anyone adds a session to the fixtures. Point 2 is the one worth measuring. `products/category/[slug]/page.tsx` carries a long comment justifying `priority={i < 3}` from LCP medians — 2892ms against 4048 at 1440 — and a fourth preload competing for the same connection is not accounted for in any of it, because none of those measurements were taken signed in. ## Why it has not shown up Every journey runs signed out. `playwright.config.ts` sets no `storageState`, and the auth journeys sign in within their own tests rather than establishing a shared session. So the header renders its signed-out branch in every measurement this repository has taken of those pages. ## Suggested direction `next/image` with an explicit `sizes` would fix 1 and 2 together, but the avatar `src` is an external URL, so it needs a `remotePatterns` entry in `next.config.js` — which is a decision about which origins this app will proxy images from, not a mechanical swap. That is the part worth deciding rather than assuming. If proxying is unwanted, `loading="lazy"` alone removes the preload and leaves the bytes unoptimised, which addresses the interference without the config question. ## Related - #230, #263 — the two surfaces whose preload budgets this competes with. - #261, #262 — the other known limits of the deferral work.
issues.display_title: The header avatar is a raw , so react-dom preloads it on every signed-in page

issues.title: The image optimiser can wedge on specific variants until the container is restarted
issues.body:
Found while verifying #263. Recorded because it cost a long misdiagnosis and would cost the next person the same.

## What happened

`e2e/image-delivery.spec.ts › the category grid image is sized to its box` failed twice at its 240s ceiling, on a quiet machine, alone. Its historical duration is ~58s.

The cause was not the test. At 390x900 the page never reached `readyState: complete`, and three optimiser requests sat in flight indefinitely:

```
still in flight after 12s:
  12035ms image /_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fproducts%2Ftents%2F21%2Fmain.webp&w=384&q=75
  12036ms image /_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fproducts%2Ftents%2F24%2Fmain.webp&w=384&q=75
  12035ms image /_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fproducts%2Ftents%2F25%2Fmain.webp&w=384&q=75
```

Outside the browser, the same three returned **nothing at all**:

```
product 21 w=384: HTTP 000 in 40.002820s     <- curl --max-time 40, no response
product 24 w=384: HTTP 000 in 40.001979s
product 25 w=384: HTTP 000 in 40.002537s
```

While, on the same process, at the same moment:

```
product 21 w=640:            HTTP 200 in 0.005171s
/images/1/242e7165-....webp  w=384: HTTP 200 in 0.146848s
```

So it is not the width, and not the image — it is a *specific (image, width) variant* that stops responding while its neighbours are served in milliseconds. No error appeared in `docker compose logs web`.

## What cleared it

`docker compose restart web`. Immediately afterwards:

```
product 21 w=384: HTTP 200 in 0.378816s
product 24 w=384: HTTP 200 in 0.163032s
product 25 w=384: HTTP 200 in 0.143939s
```

and the failing test passed in **55.1s**, against its ~58s historical baseline. The full journey suite then passed 134/134.

## What I contaminated, and what survives it

Two things I did during the investigation muddy this, and both are worth stating:

1. I ran `rm -rf .next/cache/images` **inside the running container**, which may have left the optimiser holding cache state for entries that no longer existed.
2. For a period I ran two Playwright suites against the same stack concurrently.

Neither explains the original failures, which happened **before** both. But they mean the exact trigger is not established.

What survives: a long-lived optimiser process reached a state where specific variants never respond, no log line was emitted, and only a restart recovered it.

## Why it matters beyond a flaky test

The failure mode is indefinite hang rather than error. A visitor hitting a wedged variant gets an image that never arrives and a `load` event that never fires. #230 established this optimiser is already the contended resource on these pages; this is a sharper version of the same theme — not slow, but stopped.

## Worth investigating

- Whether concurrent identical requests for one variant can deadlock on Next's in-flight dedupe.
- Whether cache-directory mutation under a running server is the trigger, which would make it self-inflicted here but still a fragility.
- Whether a request timeout in front of the optimiser would turn an indefinite hang into a failed image, which is a much better failure.

## Related

- #230 — the optimiser as a contended resource on the home page.
- #263 — the change being verified when this surfaced; it is not the cause, confirmed by the same test passing at 55.1s on a restarted container with the change in place.
issues.display_title: The image optimiser can wedge on specific variants until the container is restarted

issues.title: Does the devcontainer still work? Evidence suggests the workspace is never mounted
issues.body:
Found while moving the published host ports. Filed as a question with evidence rather than an assertion — I have not opened the devcontainer to confirm the end state.

## What is checkable without opening it

`.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`:

```json
"dockerComposeFile": "../docker-compose.yml",
"service": "web",
"workspaceFolder": "/app",
"postCreateCommand": "npm run setup:web"
```

1. **The `web` service mounts no source.** `docker-compose.yml`'s `web` has `build: .`, `ports`, `depends_on` and `environment` — and no `volumes`. So nothing binds the repository into the container.
2. **`/app` in that image is the built standalone tree**, copied at `Dockerfile:80`, not a checkout. `output: 'standalone'` in `next.config.js` means it holds a traced server bundle, not the sources.
3. **`postCreateCommand: npm run setup:web` needs the root `package.json`**, which defines that script. The runtime image does not contain it.

If those three hold, attaching gives you a shell inside a production image looking at build output, with no editable source and a post-create step that cannot run.

## What this change adds to the picture

`forwardPorts: [3000]` and `portsAttributes."3000"` were correct while `npm run dev` bound 3000 inside the container. That script is now `next dev -p 3100`, so a devcontainer user running it binds a port nothing forwards.

I did **not** update the file for that, because forwarding 3100 would be tidying a file whose larger premise is in doubt — and if the answer is "delete it", the edit is wasted.

## Worth deciding

- Whether anyone uses it. `git log` on the file will say more than I can.
- If yes: it needs a source bind mount and a workspace folder that is a checkout, and then `forwardPorts` should become 3100.
- If no: deleting it is less misleading than leaving a config that looks supported.

## Why it was not fixed in the port change

That branch moved published ports and the things coupled to them. Repairing or removing a devcontainer is a separate decision about a development surface, and it is not one I can settle from reading the file alone.
issues.display_title: Does the devcontainer still work? Evidence suggests the workspace is never mounted

issues.title: Nothing lints or type-checks the top-level scripts/ directory
issues.body:
Found by `verifier` while verifying the published-port move, and confirmed independently.

## Measured

Every Python file in the repository's top-level `scripts/` is exercised by `make test-scripts` — which runs behavioural unit tests against them — and by **no style or type gate at all**.

- Root `Makefile`'s `lint` and `typecheck` targets delegate only to `apps/web` (`$(WEB_MAKE) lint`).
- `services/chat/Makefile`'s `lint`/`typecheck` scope is `src/api tests scripts`, which is **`services/chat/scripts`** — a different directory.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` has no `ruff` or `mypy` step naming the top-level `scripts/`.

So these are unlinted: `agent_doctor.py`, `check_toolchain.py`, `check_env_contract.py`, `verify_docs.py`, `check_agent_docs.py`, `e2e_smoke.py`, `release_dry_run.py`, `detect_changed_surfaces.py`.

## How it surfaced

Running `ruff check scripts/agent_doctor.py` by hand while changing that file reported two errors:

```
EXE001  Shebang is present but file is not executable   scripts/agent_doctor.py:1
TRY004  Prefer `TypeError` exception for invalid type   scripts/agent_doctor.py:111
```

Both are **pre-existing** — confirmed by stashing the change and re-running against the committed file, which reports the identical two. They have sat there unnoticed because nothing looks.

Neither is serious in itself. The point is that nothing would have reported a serious one either.

## Why it matters here more than it looks

These scripts are not incidental tooling. `e2e_smoke.py` is the integration merge gate, `check_env_contract.py` and `check_agent_docs.py` are themselves guards, and `detect_changed_surfaces.py` decides which CI jobs run for a given change. A type error in the last of those routes the wrong checks at every pull request.

`mypy` on `agent_doctor.py` is clean today, so this is a gap rather than a backlog.

## Suggested fix

Add the directory to a lint/typecheck target and fix or explicitly ignore the two existing findings. The natural home is a root `Makefile` target that CI's Script Guardrail Tests job already has the toolchain for — it sets up Python 3.11 and would need only the `ruff`/`mypy` install.

Worth deciding at the same time whether `EXE001` should be fixed by chmod-ing the scripts or by dropping shebangs from files that are always invoked as `$(PYTHON) script.py`.
issues.display_title: Nothing lints or type-checks the top-level scripts/ directory

issues.title: Two surfaces depend on catalogue images being square, and nothing enforces it
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` while reviewing the fix for #230.

## What is unheld

`config/catalogue_images.json` and `tests/scripts/test_image_encoding.py` bound the **long edge** only. The guard reads:

```python
if max(width, height) > MAX_DIMENSION:
```

So a 1024x600 WebP satisfies every check in the repository. Nothing anywhere asserts `width == height`.

## Two rendering surfaces assume otherwise

Both put the image in a fixed-ratio box, and they fail differently:

- `apps/web/src/app/products/category/[slug]/page.tsx:47` — `aspect-square ... overflow-hidden` with the image `object-cover`. A non-square source is **cropped**, silently and plausibly, so the product's shape is wrong and nothing looks broken.
- `apps/web/src/components/listing-image.tsx` (new, from #230) — `aspect-square` on the wrapper with the image `w-full h-auto`. A non-square source is **letterboxed**, leaving a strip of `bg-zinc-200` under it.

The second one is newly introduced. The markup it replaces used `width={350} height={350}` with `h-auto`, which took its box from the source's own ratio, so it degraded gracefully. That is worth being explicit about: #230's fix traded a graceful degradation for a reserved box, and the reserved box is what makes its zero-layout-shift result true.

## Measured

All 853 files under `apps/web/public/images` referenced by the catalogue are 1024x1024 today. The one exception, 1024x450, is `hero.png`'s successor, which is on the `fullBleed` allowlist in `config/catalogue_images.json` and never reaches either surface.

So nothing renders wrong right now. The gap is that the next image someone adds has no check standing between a non-square source and a silently cropped product card.

## Suggested fix

`test_image_encoding.py` already reads both dimensions for its `maxDimension` check, so the assertion is close to free — a `width == height` check over the same corpus, with the `fullBleed` entries exempt as they already are for the other rules.

Worth deciding at the same time whether squareness belongs in `config/catalogue_images.json` as a named part of the contract, next to `quality` and `maxDimension`, rather than living only in a test. That file is described in its own `_comment` as the shared contract between the converter and the guard, and the converter does not enforce a ratio either.

## Related

- #230 -- the change that made the second surface depend on this.
- #261 -- the other known limit of that change.
issues.display_title: Two surfaces depend on catalogue images being square, and nothing enforces it

issues.title: The avatar preview's alt text describes the element, not the picture
issues.body:
On `/profile`'s General tab, `avatar-upload.tsx` renders the chosen picture with `alt="Avatar Preview"`.

That names the widget rather than describing the image, which is the same shape of defect #202 fixed on the product gallery: the alt text of a picture should say what is in it, and here nothing can — the picture is a file the visitor just chose and the app has never seen.

Two consequences.

A screen reader reading the General tab hears "Avatar Preview" where the useful information is that this *is* the current picture. Something like "Your profile picture" says what the element is for without claiming to describe what is in it.

And when the preview cannot load, the alt renders as visible text. `ui-review` photographed that while driving two overlapping uploads against #237: the frame held a revoked blob and "Avatar Preview" spilled out of the 128px circle in unstyled text. That particular route is closed — #237 made the control take one upload at a time — but any dead `src` reaches the same place, and a base64 avatar that fails to decode is one.

Not fixed in #237, which is the upload's failure handling, its announcement, and two contrast failures on the placeholder branch. This is the other branch and a wording question, so it is filed rather than folded in.
issues.display_title: The avatar preview's alt text describes the element, not the picture

issues.title: Two outlined actions, two border colours, and one dead hover state
issues.body:
Raised by `ui-review` during #231, as a convention question rather than a defect.

## The app now has two outlined actions that disagree

| control | border | text | hover |
|---|---|---|---|
| header `Sign Up` (`header.tsx:77`) | `border-indigo-600` | `text-indigo-600` | `hover:bg-indigo-50` |
| avatar upload label (`avatar-upload.tsx`) | `border-zinc-500` | `text-gray-700` | `hover:bg-gray-50` |

#231 chose the neutral deliberately — "Upload Avatar" is a secondary action and indigo would promote it visually — but that leaves the app without a settled answer for what an outlined action looks like. Worth deciding once, either direction, now that both exist.

## The neutral one has a second problem: its hover does nothing

Measured across the whole control at three viewports: **0 pixels change by the 30-unit threshold**; the largest channel-sum delta was 15, and the contrast of the change is **1.00:1**.

`bg-white` -> `hover:bg-gray-50` is `#ffffff` -> `#f9fafb`, and the page behind it is `bg-zinc-50` `#fafafa`. So on hover the control's fill moves *toward* the page, from 1.02:1 against it to about 1.00:1. It is not a weak hover state; it is a hover state that makes the control very slightly harder to see.

That matters for the border question. After #231 the avatar label is byte-identical to a text field's edge — `lab(47.8878 1.65477 -5.77283)`, 1px, 6px radius — and what separates a button from a field for a pointer user is usually that the button answers the pointer. `hover:bg-zinc-100` (`#f4f4f5`) stays neutral and moves about four times as far.

They never share a screen today: the General tab renders no fields. That is circumstance rather than design.

## Why neither was decided in #231

The colour is a decision about what the app's outlined actions look like, which is wider than one control. The hover is untouched by that change and is a separate fix on the same element.
issues.display_title: Two outlined actions, two border colours, and one dead hover state

issues.title: Focus indicators fade in, because transition-colors animates outline-color
issues.body:
Found while measuring #227 and #232.

## Measured

Tailwind v4's `transition-colors` and `transition-all` both include `outline-color`. Several controls carry one of them, so their focus outline **animates from `currentColor` to its intended colour** rather than appearing. On a white-on-indigo button `currentColor` is white, so the indicator starts invisible against a light page.

Traced on `/contact`'s Send Message, reading `outlineColor` after a programmatic focus:

```
 +0ms   solid 2px oklab(0.983956 ...)   ~white
 +50ms  solid 2px oklab(0.590642 ...)   mid-transition
+150ms  solid 2px lab(38.4009 52.6132 -92.3857)   indigo-600, settled
```

`/faq`'s Contact Support shows the same thing, and it is enough to change a measurement's verdict: screenshotted immediately after focus it reads **0 qualifying pixels**; once settled, **892 against the 876 required**.

## Why it matters

A focus indicator that takes ~150ms to become visible is a focus indicator a keyboard user does not have while they are moving. Tabbing quickly through a form, the outline may never reach full contrast before focus moves on. WCAG 2.2 2.4.13 says nothing about the time an indicator takes to appear, so this is not a violation — it is a design choice nobody appears to have made deliberately, since the transitions were added for `background-color` on hover and `outline-color` came along with them.

## Controls affected

Anything pairing `transition-colors` or `transition-all` with a `focus-visible:outline-*`. At least: `contact-form.tsx` (`transition-all`), `contact-thanks.tsx` and `faq/page.tsx` (`transition-colors`).

## Shape of the fix

`transition-[background-color]` rather than `transition-colors` on controls whose hover effect is a background change, so the outline is excluded. Or `motion-safe:` on the transition, which also answers `prefers-reduced-motion`.

## Why it was not fixed alongside #227 and #232

Those give every control a boundary and an indicator; this is about how one of them arrives. It is a separate decision, it touches `transition-*` utilities rather than the shared constant, and the fix has more than one reasonable answer.

`e2e/support/boundary.ts` now polls until the indicator stops moving before screenshotting, so the suite measures the settled state. That is deliberately not a fix — it means a regression here would still be invisible to CI.
issues.display_title: Focus indicators fade in, because transition-colors animates outline-color

issues.title: Profile tabs are unannounced, and its error and success text fail AA
issues.body:
Two more from `ui-review` during #220, both pre-existing on `/profile` and neither caused by that change.

## 1. The tabs are not tabs to a screen reader

`apps/web/src/app/profile/page.tsx:100-113` renders three `<button>`s that swap panels. None carries `role="tab"`, `aria-selected`, or an associated `role="tabpanel"`, so which section you are in is conveyed only by colour and a 2px underline.

Both are visible — active tab text `indigo-600` at 6.19:1, underline at 4.28:1, inactive `gray-500` at 4.63:1 — so this is not a contrast problem. It is that the state is never announced. A screen-reader user hears three buttons and has no way to know one of them is current.

The buttons themselves clear 2.4.13 on Chromium's default by ten pixels (448 against 438), which is a thin margin for something nothing has designed.

## 2. Error and success text fail 1.4.3

Measured against the page's rgb(250,250,250):

| | measured | AA needs |
|---|---|---|
| `text-red-500` (error) | **3.65:1** | 4.5:1 |
| `text-green-500` (success) | **2.12:1** | 4.5:1 |

The success message is the worse of the two by some way.

Neither carries `role="alert"` or `aria-live`, and no field carries `aria-invalid` or `aria-describedby` — so "Passwords do not match" is announced to nobody and names no field. After #220 all three password fields share one boundary treatment with no error variant, which means the failing field looks exactly as correct as the two beside it.

## Relationship to what is already filed

This is #218's shape on a different surface: there the finding was an invalid field being pixel-identical to a focused valid one, with the ARIA half identified as the load-bearing half. The same conclusion applies here, and #216 sharpened why — in forced colors, colour is not available to carry meaning at all, so a red-ring fix would be invisible exactly where it is needed most.

Worth deciding #218 and this together, since the answer is one pattern applied to two forms rather than two separate fixes.

## Why neither was fixed in #220

#220 changed the boundary classes on eleven text fields. Tab semantics are markup, and the error/success treatment is a decision about how failure is communicated across the app rather than a colour swap on one page.
issues.display_title: Profile tabs are unannounced, and its error and success text fail AA

issues.title: The workflow has no step for handling review comments on an open pull request
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` while reviewing the removal of the Codex reviewer from the runbook.

## What is missing

After that removal, `AGENTS.md`'s development workflow goes:

- step 10 — create the pull request from the reviewed state
- step 11 — merge only clean, passing pull requests

Nothing in between. The deleted step 11 was written around one specific bot, but it carried one instruction that was not specific to it at all: **address what a review raises, reply with what changed and what was measured, resolve the thread, and treat findings as real — arguing back with a measurement rather than complying when one is wrong.**

That applies to a human reviewer, to a different bot, or to a comment someone leaves three days later. Right now the runbook says nothing about any of them.

## Why it was not fixed in the removal

The change was scoped to taking the Codex reviewer out. Writing a general review-response step back in is adding a rule about how contributors handle feedback, not removing one — a decision about other people's behaviour, which is the repository owner's to make rather than something to slip into a deletion.

The standard `AGENTS.md` already sets for sub-agent findings is the natural source: *"Their findings are claims, not verdicts... where one is wrong, say so with the measurement rather than complying."* A pull request step could simply point at it.

## Worth deciding

- Whether this repository, which self-merges, wants such a step at all. It may be that step 11's merge gate is the whole of it.
- If so, whether the sub-agent standard should be lifted out of `### Sub-agents this workflow depends on` and stated once for any reviewer, rather than restated per surface.
issues.display_title: The workflow has no step for handling review comments on an open pull request

issues.title: "No image available" leads the accessible name of every image-less product card
issues.body:
Raised by `ui-review` during #200 as a judgement call left open rather than a defect.

## What happens

`apps/web/src/app/products/category/[slug]/page.tsx` renders a card as one link. When `product.image` is null the image slot is a placeholder reading "No image available", which sits inside that link and therefore leads its accessible name:

```
link "No image available TrailMaster X4 Tent $250.00"
```

Asserted in `page.test.tsx` (`names a product card once when it has no image`), so this is the measured string and not a reading of the markup.

#200 removed the duplication that used to be here — the placeholder's `aria-label` read `No image available for ${product.name}`, repeating the heading two lines down — and left the placeholder text itself in the name, which is where the open question is.

## The question

In a screen reader's links list, every image-less product sorts and reads under "No…" rather than under its own name. The placeholder is a visual affordance: it tells a sighted user why the frame is empty. Whether it is part of what the link *is* is a different matter.

`aria-hidden="true"` on the placeholder would drop it from the name and leave the visible text alone. It does not engage 2.5.3 Label in Name, because the placeholder is not the link's visible label — the heading below it is.

Against that: a screen-reader user then gets no signal that this product has no picture, where a sighted user does.

I lean toward hiding it. Neither answer is wrong enough to make the current behaviour a defect, which is why this is filed rather than decided inside #200.

## Not reachable from the route

No seeded product has a null `image`, so nothing renders this outside `page.test.tsx`. Same blocker as #210, and the same fix would serve both: a seeded product with no image would let a journey exercise the branch.

## Why it was not decided in #200

#200's scope was the name being announced twice, which is settled. What the placeholder should contribute to the name is a new decision about what users hear, not a continuation of that one.
issues.display_title: "No image available" leads the accessible name of every image-less product card

issues.title: Category card's no-image placeholder text is 3.91:1, failing WCAG 1.4.3
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #200, and confirmed independently.

## Measured

`apps/web/src/app/products/category/[slug]/page.tsx` — the empty state a card falls back to when `product.image` is null:

```
text  text-gray-500  lab(47.7841 -0.393182 -10.0268)  ->  rgb(106,114,130)
ground bg-gray-200   lab(91.6229 -0.159115 -2.26791)  ->  rgb(229,231,235)
14px, weight 400  ->  3.91:1
```

WCAG 2.2 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), Level AA, asks 4.5:1 of text below 18.66px bold / 24px regular. This is 14px regular, so 4.5:1 applies.

`text-gray-600` measures about 5.9:1 on the same ground and is the first step on the scale that clears it.

## How it was measured

Painted on a 1x1 canvas and read back, not parsed from the computed string. Both colours serialise as `lab()` with negative components, which is the exact shape that produced a wrong contrast reading in #184 — a numeric regex drops the minus signs and every Tailwind colour reads darker than it is.

For scale, measured in the same pass: the card price is `#6a7282` at 18px/500 on `#fafafa`, 4.63:1, which passes on a thin margin.

## Cannot be reached from the route

No seeded product has a null `image`, so this branch never renders from `/products/category/<slug>`. The measurement above is on the element reconstructed in the page from the classes in `page.tsx`. `page.test.tsx` renders the branch, but jsdom computes no colours, so a guard there cannot see this.

That is the interesting part of the issue: a fix wants a way to exercise the branch. Either the seed grows a product with no image — which would also un-block the e2e half of #200's coverage — or the colour pair is checked without rendering the route.

## Why it was not fixed in #200

#200 is about what these cards announce, not what they look like; the diff touched this element's ARIA and not its classes. Filing rather than widening a reviewed diff, per the runbook.

issues.title: The header's profile link announces the signed-in user's name twice
issues.body:
Found by sweeping every `alt=` in `apps/web/src` during #200, which is the same defect on the two product listings. ## Where `apps/web/src/components/header.tsx:35-59`. When `status === "authenticated"` the whole profile block is one `Link`: ```tsx
{session.user?.name || session.user?.email}
{session.user?.email}
``` Everything inside a link contributes to that link's accessible name, so the name reads: ``` " " ``` The avatar's `alt` says what the first line of the link already says. `title="Profile Settings"` contributes nothing here — `title` is only consulted when no other name source exists — so the one string that would tell a screen-reader user where the link goes is the one thing it does not announce. ## Not measured Read from source, not from the accessibility tree. Unlike the listings in #200 this needs a signed-in session to render, so confirming it means seeding a user and authenticating. The accname computation is not ambiguous — `alt` text contributes to an ancestor link's name — but the exact string should be read off the running build before the fix is called done. ## Shape of the fix `alt=""`: the avatar is decorative next to text that already names the user, exactly as in #200. That is a separate question and not part of this. ## Why it was not fixed in #200 Different surface and a different state. #200 is the two anonymous product listings and is covered by `e2e/browse.spec.ts`, which never signs in; this one has no journey that reaches it. issues.title: The 20 products on the home page are the ones whose gallery images say nothing
issues.body:
Raised by the Codex reviewer on #202 and, independently, by `ui-review` during the same work. Both landed on the same asymmetry from opposite directions.

## The state after #181

#181 gave gallery images alt text derived from their filename's shot type, and marked images decorative where no label exists. That leaves:

| | products | gallery images | what a screen reader hears |
|---|---|---|---|
| labelled filenames | 190 | 749 | product name, then "another angle", "detail view", "in use" |
| UUID filenames | 20 | 102 | the product name once, then **82 images announcing nothing** |

## Why this is the wrong 20

Those twenty are the seeded storefront — **every product link on the home page is one of them**. So the branch that says "nothing here knows what this picture shows" is the default experience, not an edge case. A sighted visitor on the landing path gets five photographs; a screen-reader visitor on the same path gets one sentence.

## Why it was not fixed in #181

This is option 3 from #181 — author real alt text per image — which the issue named as "data the catalogue does not currently hold", and it still does not. `alt=""` was chosen over inventing descriptions, and `ui-review` confirmed after looking at the pictures that there is no differentiating fact in them that words could carry without someone looking. WCAG H67 covers exactly this: an image whose informational content is unknown is correctly removed from the tree rather than given a guess.

That is the honest answer to "what do we say", and it is still a gap. The reviewer on #202 put it plainly: a UUID filename means no description is encoded in the path, not that the image is decorative.

## What closing this needs

Somewhere to put the text — a field on the product, or a sidecar keyed by image path — and someone to look at 102 photographs and write it. That is content work rather than a code change, which is why it is filed separately rather than folded into a reviewed diff.

If it ever gets budget, these 20 products are where it pays, not the 190 that already have shot types.
issues.display_title: The 20 products on the home page are the ones whose gallery images say nothing

issues.title: Product gallery images sit beside section headings they have nothing to do with
issues.body:
Noticed by `ui-review` during #181, while reading the product page's accessibility tree in order.

## What it looks like in reading order

```
h1  NatureNest Shelter
img "NatureNest Shelter"
h2  Features        ... eleven features ...
img "NatureNest Shelter, another angle"
h2  Reviews         ... five reviews ...
img "NatureNest Shelter, detail view"
h2  FAQ
img "NatureNest Shelter, in use"
h2  Return Policy
```

Each gallery image is interleaved with a manual section, and the pairing is arbitrary: the detail shot is announced immediately before the FAQ heading, the lifestyle shot beside Return Policy. The alt text is correct in isolation and slightly disorienting in place, because the layout implies a relationship between picture and section that does not exist.

## Why alt text is the wrong lever

#181 considered and rejected describing the images in terms of their neighbouring section — that would assert a connection nobody has checked, and would be wrong the moment the manual's sections are reordered (`page.tsx` already reorders them relative to the source markdown).

This is a layout question: a `figure`, a gallery region separate from the prose, or simply accepting the images as page furniture and marking the relationship as incidental. Whichever it is, it predates #181 and is not an accessibility failure — no criterion is violated — so it is filed rather than fixed.
