WCAG 2.2 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), Level AA, asks 4.5:1 of text. The border is now **1.9x the contrast of the hint text inside it**, which is a strange thing to ship: the box shouts and its content whispers.

`/contact` is the only one of the three forms with placeholders. `/login` and `/signup` have none.

## It also undercuts what #196 set out to do

#196's premise was that eleven fields should not style themselves independently. The ring is now identical across all eleven; the placeholder is not:

| | placeholder |
|---|---|
| chat panel input | `placeholder:text-zinc-500 placeholder:opacity-100` — 4.83:1 on white |
| the ten page fields | `placeholder:text-gray-400` — 2.60:1 on white, 2.23:1 on the contact card |

The user chose "match the chat panel exactly" for the boundary. This is the part that still does not match.

## Why it was not fixed in #196

Different criterion. #196 is 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, about a control's *boundary*; this is 1.4.3, about *text*. The constant is called `FIELD_BOUNDARY` and a placeholder is not a boundary, so folding it in would either mis-name the constant or quietly widen what it owns.

Worth deciding together with that naming: if the constant is to carry placeholder colour, disabled styling and invalid styling (see #217), it should be `FIELD_CLASSES` and say so.
issues.display_title: Contact form placeholders are 2.23:1 — weaker than the box they sit in

issues.title: The workflow has no step for handling review comments on an open pull request
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` while reviewing the removal of the Codex reviewer from the runbook.

## What is missing

After that removal, `AGENTS.md`'s development workflow goes:

- step 10 — create the pull request from the reviewed state
- step 11 — merge only clean, passing pull requests

Nothing in between. The deleted step 11 was written around one specific bot, but it carried one instruction that was not specific to it at all: **address what a review raises, reply with what changed and what was measured, resolve the thread, and treat findings as real — arguing back with a measurement rather than complying when one is wrong.**

That applies to a human reviewer, to a different bot, or to a comment someone leaves three days later. Right now the runbook says nothing about any of them.

## Why it was not fixed in the removal

The change was scoped to taking the Codex reviewer out. Writing a general review-response step back in is adding a rule about how contributors handle feedback, not removing one — a decision about other people's behaviour, which is the repository owner's to make rather than something to slip into a deletion.

The standard `AGENTS.md` already sets for sub-agent findings is the natural source: *"Their findings are claims, not verdicts... where one is wrong, say so with the measurement rather than complying."* A pull request step could simply point at it.

## Worth deciding

- Whether this repository, which self-merges, wants such a step at all. It may be that step 11's merge gate is the whole of it.
- If so, whether the sub-agent standard should be lifted out of `### Sub-agents this workflow depends on` and stated once for any reviewer, rather than restated per surface.
issues.display_title: The workflow has no step for handling review comments on an open pull request

issues.title: "No image available" leads the accessible name of every image-less product card
issues.body:
Raised by `ui-review` during #200 as a judgement call left open rather than a defect.

## What happens

`apps/web/src/app/products/category/[slug]/page.tsx` renders a card as one link. When `product.image` is null the image slot is a placeholder reading "No image available", which sits inside that link and therefore leads its accessible name:

```
link "No image available TrailMaster X4 Tent $250.00"
```

Asserted in `page.test.tsx` (`names a product card once when it has no image`), so this is the measured string and not a reading of the markup.

#200 removed the duplication that used to be here — the placeholder's `aria-label` read `No image available for ${product.name}`, repeating the heading two lines down — and left the placeholder text itself in the name, which is where the open question is.

## The question

In a screen reader's links list, every image-less product sorts and reads under "No…" rather than under its own name. The placeholder is a visual affordance: it tells a sighted user why the frame is empty. Whether it is part of what the link *is* is a different matter.

`aria-hidden="true"` on the placeholder would drop it from the name and leave the visible text alone. It does not engage 2.5.3 Label in Name, because the placeholder is not the link's visible label — the heading below it is.

Against that: a screen-reader user then gets no signal that this product has no picture, where a sighted user does.

I lean toward hiding it. Neither answer is wrong enough to make the current behaviour a defect, which is why this is filed rather than decided inside #200.

## Not reachable from the route

No seeded product has a null `image`, so nothing renders this outside `page.test.tsx`. Same blocker as #210, and the same fix would serve both: a seeded product with no image would let a journey exercise the branch.

## Why it was not decided in #200

#200's scope was the name being announced twice, which is settled. What the placeholder should contribute to the name is a new decision about what users hear, not a continuation of that one.
issues.display_title: "No image available" leads the accessible name of every image-less product card

issues.title: Category card's no-image placeholder text is 3.91:1, failing WCAG 1.4.3
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #200, and confirmed independently.

## Measured

`apps/web/src/app/products/category/[slug]/page.tsx` — the empty state a card falls back to when `product.image` is null:

```
text  text-gray-500  lab(47.7841 -0.393182 -10.0268)  ->  rgb(106,114,130)
ground bg-gray-200   lab(91.6229 -0.159115 -2.26791)  ->  rgb(229,231,235)
14px, weight 400  ->  3.91:1
```

WCAG 2.2 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), Level AA, asks 4.5:1 of text below 18.66px bold / 24px regular. This is 14px regular, so 4.5:1 applies.

`text-gray-600` measures about 5.9:1 on the same ground and is the first step on the scale that clears it.

## How it was measured

Painted on a 1x1 canvas and read back, not parsed from the computed string. Both colours serialise as `lab()` with negative components, which is the exact shape that produced a wrong contrast reading in #184 — a numeric regex drops the minus signs and every Tailwind colour reads darker than it is.

For scale, measured in the same pass: the card price is `#6a7282` at 18px/500 on `#fafafa`, 4.63:1, which passes on a thin margin.

## Cannot be reached from the route

No seeded product has a null `image`, so this branch never renders from `/products/category/<slug>`. The measurement above is on the element reconstructed in the page from the classes in `page.tsx`. `page.test.tsx` renders the branch, but jsdom computes no colours, so a guard there cannot see this.

That is the interesting part of the issue: a fix wants a way to exercise the branch. Either the seed grows a product with no image — which would also un-block the e2e half of #200's coverage — or the colour pair is checked without rendering the route.

## Why it was not fixed in #200

#200 is about what these cards announce, not what they look like; the diff touched this element's ARIA and not its classes. Filing rather than widening a reviewed diff, per the runbook.
issues.display_title: Category card's no-image placeholder text is 3.91:1, failing WCAG 1.4.3

issues.title: The header's profile link announces the signed-in user's name twice
issues.body:
Found by sweeping every `alt=` in `apps/web/src` during #200, which is the same defect on the two product listings. ## Where `apps/web/src/components/header.tsx:35-59`. When `status === "authenticated"` the whole profile block is one `Link`: ```tsx
{session.user?.name || session.user?.email}
{session.user?.email}
``` Everything inside a link contributes to that link's accessible name, so the name reads: ``` " " ``` The avatar's `alt` says what the first line of the link already says. `title="Profile Settings"` contributes nothing here — `title` is only consulted when no other name source exists — so the one string that would tell a screen-reader user where the link goes is the one thing it does not announce. ## Not measured Read from source, not from the accessibility tree. Unlike the listings in #200 this needs a signed-in session to render, so confirming it means seeding a user and authenticating. The accname computation is not ambiguous — `alt` text contributes to an ancestor link's name — but the exact string should be read off the running build before the fix is called done. ## Shape of the fix `alt=""`: the avatar is decorative next to text that already names the user, exactly as in #200. Worth deciding at the same time whether the link should announce where it goes rather than who is signed in, since `title` currently promises "Profile Settings" and delivers nothing. Note this is a raw ``, not `next/image`. That is a separate question and not part of this. ## Why it was not fixed in #200 Different surface and a different state. #200 is the two anonymous product listings and is covered by `e2e/browse.spec.ts`, which never signs in; this one has no journey that reaches it. Filing rather than widening a reviewed diff, per the runbook.
issues.display_title: The header's profile link announces the signed-in user's name twice

issues.title: The 20 products on the home page are the ones whose gallery images say nothing
issues.body:
Raised by the Codex reviewer on #202 and, independently, by `ui-review` during the same work. Both landed on the same asymmetry from opposite directions.

## The state after #181

#181 gave gallery images alt text derived from their filename's shot type, and marked images decorative where no label exists. That leaves:

| | products | gallery images | what a screen reader hears |
|---|---|---|---|
| labelled filenames | 190 | 749 | product name, then "another angle", "detail view", "in use" |
| UUID filenames | 20 | 102 | the product name once, then **82 images announcing nothing** |

## Why this is the wrong 20

Those twenty are the seeded storefront — **every product link on the home page is one of them**. So the branch that says "nothing here knows what this picture shows" is the default experience, not an edge case. A sighted visitor on the landing path gets five photographs; a screen-reader visitor on the same path gets one sentence.

## Why it was not fixed in #181

This is option 3 from #181 — author real alt text per image — which the issue named as "data the catalogue does not currently hold", and it still does not. `alt=""` was chosen over inventing descriptions, and `ui-review` confirmed after looking at the pictures that there is no differentiating fact in them that words could carry without someone looking. WCAG H67 covers exactly this: an image whose informational content is unknown is correctly removed from the tree rather than given a guess.

That is the honest answer to "what do we say", and it is still a gap. The reviewer on #202 put it plainly: a UUID filename means no description is encoded in the path, not that the image is decorative.

## What closing this needs

Somewhere to put the text — a field on the product, or a sidecar keyed by image path — and someone to look at 102 photographs and write it. That is content work rather than a code change, which is why it is filed separately rather than folded into a reviewed diff.

If it ever gets budget, these 20 products are where it pays, not the 190 that already have shot types.
issues.display_title: The 20 products on the home page are the ones whose gallery images say nothing

issues.title: Product gallery images sit beside section headings they have nothing to do with
issues.body:
Noticed by `ui-review` during #181, while reading the product page's accessibility tree in order.

## What it looks like in reading order

```
h1  NatureNest Shelter
img "NatureNest Shelter"
h2  Features        ... eleven features ...
img "NatureNest Shelter, another angle"
h2  Reviews         ... five reviews ...
img "NatureNest Shelter, detail view"
h2  FAQ
img "NatureNest Shelter, in use"
h2  Return Policy
```

Each gallery image is interleaved with a manual section, and the pairing is arbitrary: the detail shot is announced immediately before the FAQ heading, the lifestyle shot beside Return Policy. The alt text is correct in isolation and slightly disorienting in place, because the layout implies a relationship between picture and section that does not exist.

## Why alt text is the wrong lever

#181 considered and rejected describing the images in terms of their neighbouring section — that would assert a connection nobody has checked, and would be wrong the moment the manual's sections are reordered (`page.tsx` already reorders them relative to the source markdown).

This is a layout question: a `figure`, a gallery region separate from the prose, or simply accepting the images as page furniture and marking the relationship as incidental. Whichever it is, it predates #181 and is not an accessibility failure — no criterion is violated — so it is filed rather than fixed.
issues.display_title: Product gallery images sit beside section headings they have nothing to do with

issues.title: The filled send button is an emphatic no-op on an empty field
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #184, which filled the send button. The behaviour is unchanged by that work; what changed is how it reads.

## What happens

`sendMessage` returns early when the trimmed message is empty — correct, and the trim guard is deliberate. But nothing tells the user that. Clicking send with an empty field at 390 and at 1440 produces no message, no hint, no announcement, and no change in the turn count.

An outlined neutral button was a quiet affordance. A filled sky-700 button is now the most emphatic element on the surface and reads as "press this", so making it a silent no-op is a dead end the outline did not advertise.

## Suggested shape

Bind `aria-disabled={!message.trim()}` and a muted fill to the same condition.

`aria-disabled` rather than `disabled`: the panel is a focus trap below `lg`, and dropping a stop out of the tab cycle is its own problem. `aria-disabled` keeps the control focusable and announced while communicating that it will not act.

## Two smaller notes from the same review

- **Hover is a weak signal.** `hover:bg-sky-800` against `bg-sky-700` is **1.28:1**. Nothing in WCAG governs hover contrast and `cursor-pointer` carries most of the load, so this is a nit — but the hover state is close to invisible on its own. Worth knowing it was measured rather than assumed.
- **`sky-700` is written as a literal in two files.** `chat.tsx` (the send fill) and `turn.tsx` (the shopper's bubbles) resolve to the same `rgb(0, 105, 168)` and mean the same thing: "the shopper". They read as a system rather than a collision, which is right — but one concept spelled twice in two files is the setup that produced #196. A shared token would fix both.
issues.display_title: The filled send button is an emphatic no-op on an empty field

issues.title: Chat launcher's focus indicator sits on the 3:1 line against dark photography
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` during #190, and deliberately not fixed there.

## Measured

At **667×375** on `/`, where the launcher sits on the dark hero photograph, the background immediately outside its rings reads `[12,12,17]`–`[23,16,18]`. Against that, `focus-visible:outline-indigo-600` computes **2.89–3.01:1**.

WCAG 2.2 1.4.11 asks 3:1 of a focus indicator's boundary, so this is on the line and partly under it.

For reference, the `sky-700` outline it replaced computed 3.16–3.29:1 there — so #190 made this marginally worse while making the control itself far better (1.04:1 → 4.24:1 worst case). The regression is confined to the focus state on dark backgrounds.

## Why it was not fixed in #190

The launcher's resting appearance needed three tones to clear 3:1 on every background — a fill, a white ring, and a near-black hairline — precisely because no single colour can. The focus indicator has the same problem and needs the same answer: a two-tone outline, light against dark and dark against light.

That is a colour decision with the same visible consequences as the fill, and #190 already took one such decision back to the user. Bundling a second one into it would have meant deciding it silently.

## Note on scope

This is not specific to the launcher. Every `focus-visible:outline-sky-700` / `outline-indigo-600` in the codebase is a single-tone indicator, and the ones inside the chat panel sit on white so they are comfortably fine. Only the launcher floats over arbitrary backgrounds. A fix could be launcher-only, or a shared focus treatment.

`e2e/chat-launcher.spec.ts` measures the resting state only; whatever fixes this should extend it to the focused state, which is a matter of calling `.focus()` before sampling.
issues.display_title: Chat launcher's focus indicator sits on the 3:1 line against dark photography

issues.title: Nothing below the home hero is on screen in landscape; min-h-80 floors the band at 320px
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` during #162, and left open there because closing it needs `min-h-80` revisited rather than more type scaling.

## Measured

The hero band does not start at the top of the page — `Header` renders a 48px block above it. So the band being shorter than the viewport is not the same as anything below the hero being visible.

| viewport | header | band | band bottom | viewport | first `h2` top |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 667×375 | 48 | 344 | **392** | 375 | 424 |
| 844×390 | 48 | 320 | 368 | 390 | 400 |
| **568×320** (iPhone SE landscape) | 48 | 344 | **392** | 320 | — |

At 667×375 the band's bottom edge is 17px below the fold and the first category heading is 49px below that: the first screen is still entirely hero. At 568×320 the band alone is **108% of the viewport**.

#162 improved all of these substantially — 667×375 went from 424px (113%) to 344px (92%) — but did not close them.

## Why it is not a type-scale problem

`min-h-80` floors the band at **320px**. A 320px-tall viewport can never satisfy "the band is shorter than the viewport", and a 375px one cannot satisfy "the band's bottom edge is above the fold" once the 48px header and 96px of `py-12` are counted: 48 + 320 = 368 leaves 7px, before any text.

So the levers are the floor and the padding, not the font sizes:

1. **Make `min-h-80` height-aware** — drop or reduce the floor at short viewports, e.g. a `min-h-[50svh]`-style value, so the band is allowed to be as short as its content.
2. **Make the padding height-aware** — `py-12` is 96px of a 320px viewport. A smaller vertical rhythm at short heights buys most of the gap.
3. **Accept it in landscape**, and say so, on the grounds that a phone held sideways to browse a shop is uncommon.

## Guard

`e2e/layout.spec.ts` has `the home hero band is shorter than a landscape viewport`, which asserts the weaker of the two properties at 667×375 and 844×390. Its comment states plainly that it is the weaker one and points here. **568×320 is deliberately not in that list** — it would fail today.

Whatever fixes this should tighten that test to the band's bottom edge and add 568×320.
issues.display_title: Nothing below the home hero is on screen in landscape; min-h-80 floors the band at 320px

issues.title: Home hero body copy runs 95 characters a line at desktop
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #162, and deliberately left alone there because it is pre-existing desktop behaviour and #162's scope was the narrow end.

## Measured

The hero body paragraph is `w-2/3` from `md` up, which is a fraction where the constraint is really a measure:

| viewport | body box | characters on line 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 768×1024 | 496px | 57 |
| 1023×800 | 666px | 85 |
| 1024×768 | 667px | 73 |
| 1280×800 | 837px | **95** |
| 1440×900 | 837px | **95** |

45–75 characters is the comfortable range. Two thirds of a 1440px container is 837px, and at `text-lg` that is about 95 characters — the line is long enough that the eye loses its place returning to the left margin.

#162 fixed the opposite end of the same expression: `w-2/3` had been applied at *every* width, so on a 320px screen the paragraph was a 197px column. It is now `w-full md:w-2/3`, which fixed 320–767 and left the fraction doing what it always did above that.

## The fix, if taken

Replace the fraction with a measure — `max-w-[65ch]` or similar — so the paragraph stops growing once it is comfortable rather than tracking the container forever. That would visibly narrow the hero paragraph at 1280 and up, which is why it was not folded into #162: the desktop hero was explicitly unchanged there.

The subhead has the same shape (88 characters on one 20px line at 1023) and `text-balance` now handles its wrap but not its measure.
issues.display_title: Home hero body copy runs 95 characters a line at desktop

issues.title: Chat card at 1024 reads as an untitled centred dialog, and header buttons are 36x36 against Send's 44x44
issues.body:
Two presentation findings from the rendered reviews during #183. Neither is a conformance failure; both are polish at the card widths.

## 1. 1024 is the weakest width of the six

Measured at 1024×800 with the panel open: card is 650×688 at x=326–976, covering **54.6%** of the viewport, leaving a 326px sliver of page on the left and 48px on the right, and bisecting the header's Sign Up button.

It has no heading — `isCompact` is false, so the `<h2>` added in #129 is not rendered.

#183 moved the modal boundary to `lg` on the argument that "a card is only a card if the page is still there around it" (70–75% coverage at 640–834 was not). At 1024 that argument is weakest on its own terms: 54.6% does not read as a corner card, it reads as a centred dialog missing its backdrop, and it is untitled.

Options: render the title at all widths; cap the card's height so it is genuinely a corner; or accept that 1024 is the awkward end of a range that is fine by 1280.

## 2. Icon button sizes are inconsistent within the panel

Measured at 390, 834 and 1440, unchanged across them:

| control | size |
|---|---|
| Send message | 44×44 |
| launcher | 40×40 |
| Clear conversation | 36×36 |
| Close chat (sheet header) | 36×36 |

All clear WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum, AA, 24×24) comfortably. 36×36 misses 2.5.5 (AAA, 44×44). The real complaint is that three adjacent controls in one panel are three different sizes.

## Not included

The forward-Tab behaviour at `lg`+ — Tab off the last widget control puts focus on `<body>` with the panel still open, and it closes on the next keystroke — is deliberate and documented in `chat.tsx`. In a real browser that stop is the browser's own chrome, and dismissing the panel while the user is in the address bar would be wrong.
issues.display_title: Chat card at 1024 reads as an untitled centred dialog, and header buttons are 36x36 against Send's 44x44

issues.title: Chat card covers product links for mouse users at 1024+; close-on-focus-out is keyboard-only
issues.body:
Split out of #183. The fix there closes the panel when **focus** leaves it, which satisfies WCAG 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured) because that criterion is about the focused control. It does nothing for a pointer user.

## Measured

At `lg` and up, with the panel open, walking the home page in 80%-viewport scroll steps and counting links fully covered at some scroll position:

| viewport | links fully covered | card coverage |
|---|---|---|
| 1024×800 | **7 of 22** | 54.6% |
| 1440×900 | **6 of 22** | 39.5% |

Clicking bare page background fires no `focusin`, so the panel stays open: measured `{"tag":"BODY","dialogOpen":true}`. There is no pointer gesture that dismisses it except the close button itself.

Note 1024 is the worse case, not 1440 — the card is a fixed 650px wide, so the narrower the viewport above the breakpoint, the more of the page it eats.

## Why it was not fixed in #183

The decision there was that the panel is non-modal at `lg` and up, deliberately, so the site navigation stays reachable. Closing on focus-out was chosen because it reaches zero for the criterion under test. Extending it to pointer users needs a separate decision, because the obvious mechanisms all have costs:

1. **Close on outside click.** Standard popover behaviour, and it makes the panel genuinely non-blocking. But a stray click anywhere on the page discards the open chat, and clicks on page background are common.
2. **A dismiss affordance that is not the close button** — click-outside on the scrim only, or a drag handle. Needs a scrim, which #129 deliberately does not have at these widths.
3. **Shrink the card** so it covers less. Reduces the count without reaching zero, and does not help at 1024 where the card is proportionally largest.
4. **Accept it.** The links are reachable by closing the panel first, which is one click.

## Related

- #183 has the full width-by-width coverage table.
- The `chat.tsx` comment on the focus-out effect records this limitation and points here.
issues.display_title: Chat card covers product links for mouse users at 1024+; close-on-focus-out is keyboard-only

issues.title: Chat error replies are indistinguishable from real answers
issues.body:
Found during the rendered review for #129. Pre-existing.

## What happens

When a chat request fails, `chat.tsx` renders:

> Sorry, something went wrong. Please try again.

as an ordinary assistant turn — same `zinc-200` bubble, same Jane Doe avatar, same position in the log. There is no error affordance, no icon, no colour change, and no retry control.

Reproduced at 390 both by aborting `/api/chat/service` and naturally, since the local backend returns 500 without a configured LLM provider.

## Why it matters

At a glance it reads as an answer. A user who asked "which tent for two people in winter?" gets something in the assistant's voice, in the assistant's bubble, and has to read it to discover nothing happened. Retrying means retyping the question — the message has already been sent and cleared from the input.

The component distinguishes these states internally already: `settleWithError` produces this turn, and `ChatTurn` carries a `status`. Nothing surfaces the difference.

## Worth deciding

- A distinct error presentation (border, icon, `role="alert"` rather than the polite log).
- A retry that resends the question that failed, rather than making the user retype it.
- Whether the failed question should stay in the input on error instead of being cleared.
issues.display_title: Chat error replies are indistinguishable from real answers

issues.title: At tablet width the category grid's priority cutoff splits a visible row, so adjacent cards arrive 2.7s apart
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` on `perf/prioritise-lcp-images` (#169). A known, measured consequence of the cutoff that PR chose, filed rather than fixed because the alternatives are worse on the numbers.

## What it looks like

`priority={i < 3}` preloads the first three cards. At **834×1112** the grid is two columns, so cards 3 and 4 sit side by side with **251px of each above the fold** — and card 3 is index 2 (eager) while card 4 is index 3 (lazy).

Median load completion over three throttled runs (1.6 Mbps / 150 ms RTT / 4× CPU):

```
card 3 (eager)  1295 ms
card 4 (lazy)   3980 ms
```

A **2.7-second gap between two adjacent, equally visible cards in the same row.** The rendered filmstrip at 2200 ms shows three tents painted and a bare grey box beside the third.

At 1440 the equivalent band is cards 4–6 with 63px visible, and they are uniformly late, which reads as "there is more below" rather than as something broken. At 390 there is no artifact — nothing below card 1 is on screen.

## Why #169 shipped it anyway

`priority` cannot vary by viewport, so one cutoff serves all three layouts. Measured LCP by cutoff, median of 7:

| width | n=0 | n=1 | n=2 | **n=3** | n=6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 390 | 1540 | **736** | 744 | 748 | 840 |
| 834 | 2380 | **1404** | 1480 | 1488 | 1588 |
| 1440 | 2836 | 2972 | 1816 | **1788** | 1900 |

Summed regret against the best value at each width: n=1 costs 1184 ms, n=2 costs 112, **n=3 costs 96**, n=6 costs 400. So 3 is the best available single number, and 6 — which would cover the visible rows at 1440 — is worse everywhere.

Note n=1 is *worse than doing nothing* at 1440.

## Options

1. **Accept it.** The artifact is at one breakpoint band, it is a delay rather than a defect, and CLS is 0.0000 throughout because the `aspect-square` wrapper reserves the box. This is where #169 left it.
2. **A hand-rolled responsive preload.** `<link rel="preload" as="image" media="...">` can vary by viewport where `priority` cannot. Measured ceiling on the gain: **84 ms at 834 and 12 ms at 390**. Real machinery for very little.
3. **Cut at 4.** Untested. It would pair cards 3 and 4 correctly at 834 and cost phones a third off-screen preload; the n=6 row suggests the cost curve is already rising.

(1) unless someone finds the tablet band jarring in practice.

## Worth knowing

`next/image`'s `priority` sets no `fetchpriority` in Next 16.2 — it only flips `loading` and emits a preload link. So preloaded cards compete with the LCP element on equal terms, which is the mechanism behind both the n=1 regression and this artifact.
issues.display_title: At tablet width the category grid's priority cutoff splits a visible row, so adjacent cards arrive 2.7s apart

issues.title: maxDimension is one knob for two populations: the catalogue guard and the srcset ceiling
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` on `perf/optimise-background-images` (#158). Not a defect today — nothing is wrong at the current values — but the coupling is now load-bearing in a way it was not before, and the next person to hit it will be given bad options.

## The coupling

`config/catalogue_images.json`'s `maxDimension: 1024` does two unrelated jobs:

1. **A guard.** `tests/scripts/test_image_encoding.py` fails any governed image wider than it.
2. **A delivery ceiling.** `apps/web/next.config.js` derives `deviceSizes` from it — default rungs below the source width, plus the first at or above.

Those were the same decision while the only governed images were catalogue photographs rendered at 350 and 550. #158 moved the two full-bleed backgrounds into the governed set, and they are not that.

## What goes wrong

The hero is upscaled **2.81× at desktop 2× and 5.0× at 2560**. The obvious fix is a sharper source — a 2048px hero. That now fails the guard, and raising `maxDimension` to admit it would:

- **relax the guard for all 854 images**, including the catalogue it was written for
- **re-add duplicate srcset candidates**: the ladder goes `[640,750,828,1080]` → `[640,750,828,1080,1200,1920,2048]`, and since every catalogue source is 1024 wide, `w=1080/1200/1920/2048` all return byte-identical bytes. Four cache entries per image where there is one today, across 854 images — precisely the waste #150 removed
- **gain the background nothing**, because a CSS `background-image` URL never reaches the optimiser, so no srcset rung applies to it at all

So the one knob is shared between a population that needs it low and a population the delivery half cannot serve.

## Options

1. **Split the field.** `maxDimension` stays the guard's ceiling; a separate value — or a derivation that does not read it — feeds `next.config.js`. Cleanest, and makes each number answerable on its own terms.
2. **A dimension-only exemption for full-bleed art.** Keeps format and weight governance, which is where the exemption was doing nothing useful, and drops the dimension check, which is where it was earning its keep. Costs a second list, which the current comment deliberately avoided.
3. **Leave it.** Nothing is broken; both backgrounds are exactly 1024. The failure message on the dimension check now spells out all three consequences above, so a maintainer who hits it is at least warned rather than misdirected.

(3) is where #158 left it, deliberately. (1) is the right answer whenever someone actually wants a sharper background.

## Related

#165 already records that `fullBleed` is a misleading name for the remaining exemption. This is the other half of the same tidy-up: the field name is wrong, and the field it sits next to does two jobs.
issues.display_title: maxDimension is one knob for two populations: the catalogue guard and the srcset ceiling

issues.title: No e2e check watches network failures on /contact, so its background image is unguarded at runtime
issues.body:
Found by `verifier` on `perf/optimise-background-images` (#158), correcting a claim I had made twice — including in #158 itself.

## What I said, and why it was wrong

I described `apps/web/e2e/browse.spec.ts`'s image check as inspecting "only `img` and `/_next/image` traffic, so a CSS background that 404s is invisible to it".

That is not what it does, and I wrote the code that makes it not so. The pattern is:

```ts
const IMAGE_REQUEST = /\/_next\/image\?|\.(png|jpe?g|webp|gif|svg)(\?|$)/i
```

The second alternation matches any URL ending in an image extension — which is exactly how a CSS `background-image` is fetched. The comment directly above it says as much: *"Only the CSS backgrounds are fetched by path"*. `verifier` confirmed empirically that navigating to `/` fires a real response event for `/images/hero.webp` that this check would catch if it 404'd.

So **`hero.webp` is guarded at runtime.**

## The real gap

`contact-bg.webp` is not — but for a different reason than a pattern gap. **No spec that listens for response failures ever visits a page that uses it.**

- `browse.spec.ts` has the listener, and visits `/` only
- `headings.spec.ts` visits `/contact`, but asserts on the heading outline, not on network status
- `/contact/thanks` is visited by no e2e spec at all

Both pages do fire real 200 requests for `contact-bg.webp` today, so the coverage would work — there is just nothing there to observe it.

This predates #158: the same hole existed when the file was `contact-bg.jpg`, and that change neither widened nor narrowed it.

## Suggested

The cheapest fix is to give the existing check more than one route. It currently hard-codes `/`; iterating a small list — `/`, `/contact`, `/contact/thanks`, `/about` — would cover every path-fetched image the app has, and the assertion machinery already exists.

Worth doing before another background image lands on a route nothing watches.

## Worth recording

The mistake underneath this is worth more than the gap. I asserted a limitation of a check I had written myself, in a comment that contradicted me, and repeated it into an issue and two review briefs without re-reading the code. Nobody caught it until a verifier went and looked. Same shape as the documentation defects on #152 and #161: prose about a check, believed because it was written down.
issues.display_title: No e2e check watches network failures on /contact, so its background image is unguarded at runtime

issues.title: Contact page heading and subheading fall below WCAG AA against the busiest parts of the background
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` on `perf/optimise-background-images` (#158). **Pre-existing and identical before and after that change** — the re-encode moves contrast by at most 0.16 ratio points — so it is not a regression, but it is the one real contrast problem on a page that PR touches.

## Measured

Worst-pixel ratio against the actual rendered background, with glyphs hidden and the background sampled underneath:

| element | required | phone | tablet | desktop | mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "Get in Touch" (large text) | 3.0 | 4.89 | 3.22 | **2.87** | 7.3–9.6 |
| "Ready for your next adventure?" (20px/400) | 4.5 | **2.94** | **2.53** | **3.43** | 7.3–8.0 |

`apps/web/src/app/contact/page.tsx`. The subheading is below AA at all three viewports; the heading at desktop.

## Why the mean is misleading here

The mean ratio is comfortable everywhere — 7.3 and up. Text over a photograph is not judged against the mean: it is judged against the brightest region it actually overlaps, because that is where the glyphs disappear. The existing `bg-gray-900/40` wash and 2px backdrop blur lift the average without flattening the highlights.

`/contact/thanks` is fine — 14.6 and 6.2 — because its copy sits on an opaque card rather than directly on the image.

## Options

1. **Deepen the wash behind the heading block specifically** — a local gradient or a second scrim over just that region, leaving the rest of the image as it is.
2. **Give the heading and subheading a text shadow or a local scrim.** The heading already has `drop-shadow-md` and the subheading `drop-shadow-xs`; those are shadows for depth, not for contrast, and are too soft to carry it.
3. **Raise the global wash** past 40%. Simplest, and costs the image most.

(1) or (2) keeps the photograph readable while fixing the text.

## Worth knowing

Nothing in the suite measures this. The rendered contrast check that produced these numbers samples the composited background under each text box — that is not something `ui-review` can do on every run without being asked, and there is no automated equivalent in the repo.
issues.display_title: Contact page heading and subheading fall below WCAG AA against the busiest parts of the background

issues.title: image-delivery.spec shares one width and density sweep across four surfaces, so most loads cannot fail
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` on `perf/size-home-grid-images` (#171). A design point in the spec rather than a defect, and a bigger change than that PR should carry.

## The shape

`WIDTHS` and `DENSITIES` are module constants, so every surface runs every combination — 21 widths × 2 densities = **42 page loads each**, 168 in total. But the widths are surface-specific:

- 1015, 1016, 1017, 1105, 1106 exist for the home grid
- 1224 exists for the category grid
- 574 exists for the product detail page

Each is inert on the other three surfaces.

## Worse: the home surface's entire 1× pass has no red phase

The home card is never wider than 350px and the ladder floor is 384, so at 1× **every** swept width expects `w=384` — and gets it under the shipped value, under the previous `(min-width: 640px) 350px, 45vw`, and under both intermediate values tried while fixing #171. Twenty-one of that surface's forty-two loads, roughly half its ~80s, assert something that did not fail for the bug they were added to catch.

They are not worthless — a future over-declaration beyond 384px would trip them — but that is a >9.7% error at the cap. The 2× half carries the real coverage: it fails against the old value at 900 (declared 350 → `w=750`, real box 281.33 → `w=640`) and 1015/1016 fail against the decimal variant.

This is exactly what AGENTS.md step 4 now asks to be written down — which mistake each assertion catches, and which nothing catches.

## Suggested

Move `widths` and `densities` onto the surface record, with a note per surface saying which mistake each pass catches. That takes the home surface from 42 loads to roughly 10 without losing an assertion that can fail, and cuts the whole spec well under half its current cost.

Worth doing before a fifth surface lands — the cost is multiplicative in surfaces, and #169 will likely add LCP coverage to two more.

## Related

The spec's `test.setTimeout(240_000)` exists because the slowest surface is ~80s locally. Per-surface sweeps would make that cap comfortable again rather than something to keep raising.
issues.display_title: image-delivery.spec shares one width and density sweep across four surfaces, so most loads cannot fail

issues.title: Every sizes value corrects 100vw by a pixel constant, but 100vw includes a classic scrollbar
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` on `perf/size-home-grid-images` (#171). Pre-existing across all four surfaces, and structurally invisible to the test that guards them.

## The skew

All four `sizes` strings derive the box from `100vw` less the container's padding and gaps:

- `apps/web/src/app/page.tsx` — `calc( ( 100vw - 56px ) / 3 )`, `calc( 50vw - 20px )`
- `apps/web/src/app/products/[slug]/page.tsx` — `calc( 100vw - 24px )`
- `apps/web/src/app/products/category/[slug]/page.tsx` — `calc( 100vw / 3 - 24px )` and siblings
- `apps/web/src/app/about/page.tsx` — `calc( 50vw - 36px )`, `calc( 100vw - 24px )`

On a desktop browser with **classic (non-overlay) scrollbars**, `100vw` is the layout viewport *plus* the scrollbar — roughly 15px — while the container the arithmetic describes is not. So every clause over-declares by up to ~15px times its fraction.

For the home grid that is ~5px, and between roughly 1016 and 1031 at 2× it tips into `w=750` where `w=640` covers the real box. Small window, and it errs toward over-fetch rather than softness, which is the safe direction — but it is a systematic error in all four values rather than a rounding artifact.

## Why nothing catches it

Playwright launches Chromium with `--hide-scrollbars`, so the sweep in `apps/web/e2e/image-delivery.spec.ts` measures a viewport with no scrollbar at all. That is why the home card measures 320.328 at 1017px rather than the ~315.3 a real desktop browser would produce. The entire class of skew is outside what the spec can observe.

## Options

1. **Accept it.** The direction is safe, the windows are narrow, and overlay scrollbars are now the default on macOS and on Windows 11's newer surfaces. Record it in a comment so the next person deriving a `sizes` value knows the arithmetic is approximate by construction.
2. **Use `calc( 100% ... )` where the element's containing block is the right reference.** `sizes` accepts any CSS length, and percentages there resolve against the viewport rather than the element, so this needs checking rather than assuming.
3. **Subtract a scrollbar allowance.** Wrong on the majority of devices that have no scrollbar, so it trades one error for a larger one.

(1) is probably right. The value of the issue is that the limitation is written down somewhere other than a review transcript.
issues.display_title: Every sizes value corrects 100vw by a pixel constant, but 100vw includes a classic scrollbar

issues.title: The srcset ladder is too sparse between 384 and 640, and its lower half is unreachable for full-width images
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` on `perf/size-product-images-to-their-boxes` (#166). Two separate limits of the rung ladder, both surfaced by making `sizes` accurate. Neither is a defect in that change; both cap how much accurate sizing can buy.

## 1. The 384 → 640 gap makes accuracy cost bytes in a narrow band

The category grid at **834px, 1×** got **heavier**, not lighter: 262 KB → 632 KB across 14 images (+369 KB).

The old `45vw` declared 375px for a 393px box, so the browser picked the 384 rung and upscaled it 2.3% — imperceptible, and cheap. The corrected value declares 393 honestly, and the next rung above 384 is **640**. So the fix trades a 2.3% upscale for 63% more pixels than the box needs.

That is correct behaviour and the `sizes` value should stay as it is. But it means "size images to their boxes" is not a pure win everywhere, and the reason is the ladder, not the sizing.

Affected band is roughly **817–853px** at 1×. At 900 both old and new select 640; at 390 and 1440 nothing changes at either density.

A rung near **448 or 512** would recover most of it. That is a change to `images.imageSizes` in `apps/web/next.config.js`, which is currently Next's unconfigured default — and it trades against #150, which removed redundant cache entries. Worth measuring both directions before deciding.

## 2. Full-width images can never be served below w=640

`next/image` computes `smallestRatio` from the smallest `vw` in the `sizes` string, then filters the ladder:

```js
allSizes.filter(s => s >= deviceSizes[0] * smallestRatio)
```
`apps/web/node_modules/next/dist/shared/lib/get-img-props.js:51-65`

Any `sizes` whose narrowest clause is `100vw` gets ratio 1.0, so the filter drops every rung below `deviceSizes[0]` — which is **640**. On the product detail page at 390px the box is 366, and the smallest candidate the browser is ever offered is 640: roughly 3× the pixel area needed.

Mitigating: at DPR 2 a 366px box wants 732 device pixels, so 750 is selected and nothing is wasted. The cost is confined to DPR-1 phones.

**This is invisible to `image-delivery.spec.ts`**, which asserts the request is the smallest rung *offered*. 640 is the smallest offered, so the spec passes. Worth knowing before trusting that spec as complete: it catches a `sizes` that misdescribes the box, not a ladder that cannot serve it.

There is no honest fix in `sizes` — the box really is ~100vw at phone widths. It would need a rung below 640 to be reachable, which is (1) again.

## Together

Both point at the same lever: `images.imageSizes`, currently unconfigured. Worth one measured decision covering the gap, the unreachable lower half, and the cache-entry cost #150 was about.
issues.display_title: The srcset ladder is too sparse between 384 and 640, and its lower half is unreachable for full-width images

issues.title: about/mission.png is in the fullBleed allowlist for a reason this measurement disproves
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` on `perf/about-mission-image-sizing` (#157), which measured the thing the justification asserts. Filing rather than folding in — the conclusion is unaffected, only the stated reason is wrong.

## The claim

`config/catalogue_images.json` lists `about/mission.png` under `fullBleed`, and `tests/scripts/test_image_encoding.py` describes the set as *"Two full-bleed CSS backgrounds and one `fill` image in a full-width band"*. I wrote that in #155 after correcting an earlier version that had called all three CSS backgrounds.

## Why it is wrong

The band is **not full-width**. It is one column of a `md:grid-cols-2` grid inside a `max-w-(--breakpoint-xl)` container, so it is half the container less half the gap. Measured across 35 widths while sizing #157:

```
767 -> 743   (single column below md)
768 -> 348   (grid engages, drops to half)
1280+ -> 604 (container stops growing)
```

It never exceeds **604 CSS px** — under half the viewport on a desktop, and narrower at 768 than at 767.

## The exemption still holds, for a different reason

604 CSS px at 2× needs 1208 device pixels, and the source is 1024. So it is already short of what a retina screen asks for, and downscaling it to the catalogue's `maxDimension` would make that worse. That is the real justification, and it is a stronger one than "full-bleed" — it is the same argument #96 made for keeping the catalogue at 1024.

So: keep the exemption, fix the sentence. `fullBleed` is also now a misleading name for what the list contains — something like `notCatalogue` or `exempt` would describe it honestly.

## Related

The file is still a **1.9 MB PNG on disk**, the largest single asset served through the optimiser. #158 covers the other two allowlisted images for the same reason; this one belongs in that conversation.
issues.display_title: about/mission.png is in the fullBleed allowlist for a reason this measurement disproves

issues.title: The about page's mission image alt duplicates the heading beside it
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` on `perf/about-mission-image-sizing` (#157). Pre-existing, and a content decision rather than a mechanical fix, so filing rather than guessing at it in that PR. ## What happens `apps/web/src/app/about/page.tsx:21` renders `

Our Mission

`, and line 32 gives the image immediately beside it `alt="Our Mission"`. A screen reader announces the phrase twice in a row, and the second announcement carries no information: the alt describes the heading, not the picture. The image is a photograph — hikers on a lakeside trail at sunrise, per the rendered review — and none of that reaches anyone who cannot see it. ## Two defensible answers 1. **Describe it.** Something like `alt="Hikers on a lakeside trail at sunrise"`. Right if the photograph carries meaning the copy does not. 2. **`alt=""`.** Right if it is decorative — chosen to set a mood beside the mission statement rather than to inform. That removes it from the accessibility tree entirely and stops the duplicate announcement. (2) is probably correct here: the two paragraphs beside it say what the mission is, and the image illustrates rather than adds. But that is an editorial call about what the picture is doing on the page, which is why this is an issue rather than a one-word fix. Worth checking the other decorative images on the same page and on `/contact` at the same time.
issues.display_title: The about page's mission image alt duplicates the heading beside it

issues.title: test_agent_definitions only guards agent names below one heading, so names elsewhere in AGENTS.md can go stale
issues.body:
Found by `code-review` while reviewing the AGENTS.md change that adds *Unrelated findings become issues*. Same shape as #100, lower severity, so filing rather than widening a documentation change.

## What is unguarded

`tests/scripts/test_agent_definitions.py` exists so AGENTS.md cannot claim a sub-agent that does not exist. But `agent_names_claimed_by_docs()` splits the file at the `### Sub-agents this workflow depends on` heading and only scans below it.

The new section names all three agents above that heading:

```
`ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` read more of the repository than the
change touches.
```

Rename or remove an agent and that line goes stale with the test green.

## Why it is minor

The guarded section would fail first on the same rename, so the failure is loud and the stale line gets found while fixing it. And the claim above the heading is only a *name*, not a capability — the class of thing #100 was filed about (prose asserting behaviour nothing enforces) is not what is unguarded here.

Worth fixing when the file is next touched rather than on its own.

## Options

1. Scan the whole file for agent-name references instead of the region below one heading. Straightforward, but it widens what the test treats as a claim — mentions in prose, examples and troubleshooting all become assertions.
2. Keep the region split and add a narrower whole-file check for backticked names matching a known agent-name shape.

(1) is probably right if the false-positive rate turns out to be low; worth counting the matches across the current file before deciding.
issues.display_title: test_agent_definitions only guards agent names below one heading, so names elsewhere in AGENTS.md can go stale

issues.title: Working agreement for the autonomous maintenance loop
issues.body:
Durable context for whoever — or whatever — picks this up next. Kept as an issue rather than in an agent's local memory so it survives a cleared context and is visible to everyone.

## How this repository is being worked

Changes go through the [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md) workflow end to end: branch, implement, ui-review, verifier, code-review, PR. PRs merge when CI is green. Findings become issues. The loop continues to the next item without pausing for step-by-step approval.

The point is that it runs unattended, so stopping to confirm each step defeats it.

## What still gets surfaced rather than decided silently

Proceeding by default does not mean deciding everything. Three categories get a recommendation and a question:

1. **Changes to what users see** — image quality, layout tradeoffs. #96 is the live example: re-encoding to WebP is well-measured, but q82/600px is a judgment about acceptable fidelity, not a fact.
2. **Changes to other contributors' behavior** — #147 committed tool config that runs hooks on anyone's machine who clones. That deserved saying out loud, not just doing.
3. **Rewrites of shared history** — never silently. See the note below on why this keeps coming up.

The rest of the work does not wait on those answers. Finish everything that does not depend on the decision first, then ask.

## Two things that have repeatedly caught people out

**Checks that run without asserting on what they produced.** This is the repo's signature defect, found three separate times: the E2E smoke passed against a chat service returning `fallback: true`; the seed ran green on every PR while writing credentials that could never authenticate (#141); a category page referenced an image that had never existed (#137). A green check is not evidence unless something inspects its output.

**Verifying in a richer environment than the real one.** Also recurring: a populated local venv vs CI's bare one; jsdom vs a real browser; three sampled viewports vs the breakpoint boundaries where the defects actually live; `node_modules` vs the standalone image; a local stack reading `.env` vs CI with none. If a check passes locally, confirm it runs in the environment that matters.

**Deleting files does not shrink `git clone`.** The blobs stay reachable from history. #146 removed 68.6 MB from the working tree and the web image; `size-pack` did not move. Worth remembering before promising a clone-size win — see the measurement in #66.

## Running the stack locally

Environments differ per machine (port collisions, whether Ollama is installed for `LLM_PROVIDER=local`). `make e2e-smoke` may need a compose override for ports and provider. Resolve collisions with an override file using `ports: !override` — a plain `ports:` list appends rather than replaces — and never by stopping containers you did not start.

## Current state

`main` is clean. #145, #146 and #147 are merged. Open: #96 (WebP re-encode, the next substantive item), #66 (image weight, parent of #96), #118 (import-declaration guardrail), #129 (chat panel below `sm`, needs a design decision), #69 and #90 (blocked upstream).
issues.display_title: Working agreement for the autonomous maintenance loop

issues.title: check_dependency_policy.py cannot catch an import with no manifest entry
issues.body:
Split out of #104, which fixed the two instances. This is the guardrail that would stop the next one.

`services/chat/scripts/check_dependency_policy.py` enforces three rules today:

- `constraints.txt` pins must be exact `==`
- every manifest entry must be pinned
- every pin must be required by some manifest

All three start from a **declaration**. None of them start from an **import**. So a package that source code imports but no manifest declares is invisible to the checker — it resolves fine as long as something else happens to pull it in, and breaks silently later when that something else is removed or bumped.

This has now bitten three times:

- `httpx` — imported-but-undeclared, arriving via `prisma-client-py`. Removing prisma dropped it, and the failure surfaced later and elsewhere as a `starlette` error about `httpx2` (#57).
- `pydantic` — imported directly by `src/api/main.py`, present only via fastapi / google-cloud-aiplatform / google-genai (#104).
- `opentelemetry-exporter-gcp-trace` — imported under a `try/ImportError` guard, installed nowhere, so the feature was a permanent no-op (#104).

## Suggested rule

Every top-level module imported by service source must resolve to a declared manifest entry.

## The hard part

Import name and distribution name are not the same, and the mapping is not derivable from the manifests alone:

| import | distribution |
| --- | --- |
| `dotenv` | `python-dotenv` |
| `vertexai` | `google-cloud-aiplatform` |
| `google` | namespace spanning `google-cloud-aiplatform`, `google-auth`, `google-cloud-discoveryengine` |
| `opentelemetry` | namespace spanning `opentelemetry-api`, `opentelemetry-sdk`, `opentelemetry-instrumentation-fastapi` |

So the rule needs either an explicit alias table (deterministic, needs maintenance) or `importlib.metadata.packages_distributions()` (accurate, but only works against an installed environment, making the check environment-dependent).

Namespace packages want an "at least one of these distributions is declared" form rather than a 1:1 match.

The checker also has to exclude the standard library (`sys.stdlib_module_names`) and first-party modules (`contoso_chat`, `evaluators`, `tracing`, `local_provider_health`, ...), which are imported as bare top-level names because of how `sys.path` is set up.

## Worth deciding

Whether the same rule should cover `apps/web` imports against `package.json`. The web side has not had this failure mode, but it has the same shape.
issues.display_title: check_dependency_policy.py cannot catch an import with no manifest entry

issues.title: Revisit TypeScript 7 when typescript-eslint supports it
issues.body:
Records why TypeScript 7 is not adoptable yet, so the next Dependabot proposal can be closed against this rather than re-investigated.

## Blocker

`eslint-config-next@16.2.12` bundles `typescript-eslint@8.65.0`, whose peer range is:

```
peer typescript@">=4.8.4 <6.1.0"
```

TypeScript 7.0.2 falls outside it, and the tool refuses outright rather than degrading:

```
typescript-eslint does not support TS 7.0.
Please see https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/#running-side-by-side-with-typescript-6.0
  to run typescript-eslint using the TS 6 API.
See also https://github.com/typescript-eslint/typescript-eslint/issues/10940
  for tracking typescript-eslint's support for TS >=7.1
```

So `npm run lint` fails outright — this is not a matter of fixing type errors in our code.

## Options when revisiting

1. Wait for `typescript-eslint` to support TS >= 7.1 — tracked upstream at typescript-eslint#10940
2. Run typescript-eslint against the TS 6 API side-by-side, per the TypeScript 7 announcement. Adds a second compiler to the toolchain, which is worth avoiding unless the upgrade becomes urgent.

Option 1 is the sane default. Note it also depends on `eslint-config-next` shipping a `typescript-eslint` that supports it.

## Related

Same shape as #69 (ESLint 10 blocked by `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y`): the blocker is a transitive dependency of `eslint-config-next`, not our code. Both will keep being proposed by Dependabot until upstream moves.

Closed for now: #80.
issues.display_title: Revisit TypeScript 7 when typescript-eslint supports it

issues.title: public/images is 732 MB and dominates both the repo and the web image
issues.body:
## Problem

`apps/web/public/images` is **732 MB** of product photography committed to git.

```
$ du -sh apps/web/public/images
732M
$ git count-objects -vH | grep size-pack
size-pack: 661.54 MiB
```

It is the single largest thing in both the repository and the built web image.

## Impact

- **Web image**: the runtime image is ~1.28 GB against a 1.5 GB budget. `public/` is ~730 MB of that, so images are roughly **57% of the image** and most of the remaining headroom. Any future dependency growth pushes us over a budget that is already mostly consumed by static assets.
- **Clone/CI cost**: every clone and every CI checkout pulls 660 MB of pack.
- It already caused one incident indirectly: when Next 16 changed `standalone` to include `public/`, the duplicated copy added ~730 MB to the image in a second layer and blew the budget (fixed in #60). The duplication was only expensive *because* the directory is enormous.

## Proposed

Serve product images from object storage / a CDN rather than the app image, and keep only whatever placeholder assets the tests need in the repo.

Worth confirming first whether all 732 MB is actually referenced — `products.json` may point at a subset.

## Notes

Not urgent in the sense that nothing is broken, but this is the main reason the image budget is tight, and shrinking it buys headroom everywhere else. It also interacts with #32 (full-profile chat image), which is over its own budget for unrelated reasons.

issue.title: evaluate.py passes to_markdown's mode positionally, which pandas 4.0 removes
issue.body:
Found while verifying #294 (a `google-cloud-aiplatform` bump). Pre-existing and unrelated to that PR — it is one of the two warnings every chat test run has been printing.

## Measured

`services/chat/src/api/evaluate.py:110`:

```python
mean_df.to_markdown('eval_results.md', 'a')
```

The second positional argument is `mode`. pandas already warns on it, on every run of `make -C services/chat ci`:

```
tests/unit/test_evaluate.py::test_create_summary_writes_markdown
  services/chat/src/api/evaluate.py:110: Pandas4Warning: Starting with pandas
  version 4.0 all arguments of to_markdown except for the argument 'buf' will
  be keyword-only.
```

`pandas` is pinned at `3.0.5` in `services/chat/constraints.txt`, so nothing breaks today. It breaks the first time dependabot proposes pandas 4.x.

Line 107 two lines above is fine — `df.to_markdown('eval_results.md')` passes only `buf`.

## Fix

```python
mean_df.to_markdown('eval_results.md', mode='a')
```

## Why file it rather than leave it for the bump to find

It will be found either way: `test_create_summary_writes_markdown` covers this path, so a pandas 4 bump fails CI rather than shipping broken. But it fails as a *dependabot PR that looks like it broke something*, which is the most confusing shape for the person triaging it — the diff will be one version line and the failure will be in unrelated application code.

Fixing it now costs one keyword and turns that future PR back into a routine bump. It also removes one of exactly two warnings from the chat test output, and a suite with no warnings is one where a new warning is visible.

The other warning is filed separately — it is a transitive-dependency question rather than a line of our code.

issue.title: seed_gcp_all.py reinstalls on every run and pip-installs vertexai outside the constraints policy
issue.body:
Found by `code-review` during #294, while it was checking which files in the repository reach `vertexai`. Pre-existing and unrelated to that bump.

Two defects in `install_requirements()` in `infrastructure/scripts/seed_gcp_all.py`, lines 62-80.

## 1. The "already installed" check can never pass

```python
for package in requirements:
    try:
        importlib.import_module(package.replace('-', '_'))
        logger.debug(f"Package {package} already installed")
    except ImportError:
        logger.info(f"Installing {package}...")
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", package], ...)
```

`package.replace('-', '_')` turns `google-cloud-discoveryengine` into `google_cloud_discoveryengine`, which is not an importable module name. The real ones are `google.cloud.aiplatform` and `google.cloud.discoveryengine_v1`. Measured against a venv that has both packages installed:

```
google_cloud_aiplatform      -> ImportError: No module named 'google_cloud_aiplatform'
google_cloud_discoveryengine -> ImportError: No module named 'google_cloud_discoveryengine'
```

So the `except ImportError` branch is taken every time and the `logger.debug("already installed")` branch is unreachable. The script shells out to `pip install` on every invocation regardless of state.

Distribution names and import names are simply different namespaces, and `replace('-', '_')` is the mapping people reach for when they assume otherwise. It happens to work for flat packages, which is why it survives.

## 2. It installs `vertexai`, unpinned, outside the constraints policy

The list is:

```python
requirements = [
    "google-cloud-discoveryengine",
    "google-cloud-aiplatform",
    "vertexai"
]
```

and the install is a bare `pip install <package>` with **no `-c constraints.txt`**.

Two problems, and the second is the sharp one:

- It bypasses the dependency policy entirely. `services/chat/AGENTS.md` says "dependency versions belong in `constraints.txt`", and `check_dependency_policy.py` exists to hold that. A `pip install` with no constraint file can move any of these to any version.
- **`vertexai` is the package this repository deliberately excludes.** `services/chat/src/api/requirements-core.txt` says so explicitly, in a comment written for exactly this reason:

  > The standalone `vertexai` package is deliberately absent: it pins google-cloud-aiplatform to an exact version, which blocks every aiplatform bump. google-cloud-aiplatform ships the `vertexai` module itself.

  So running this script can pull `google-cloud-aiplatform` off its pin as a side effect — the precise outcome that comment exists to prevent, undone by a script in another directory.

Combined with (1), that install runs on every invocation rather than once.

## Fix

The presence check either wants a real distribution lookup (`importlib.metadata.version(package)`) or should be deleted — `pip install` is already idempotent, so the check is buying very little. Drop `vertexai` from the list, since `google-cloud-aiplatform` provides the module. If the install stays, it needs `-c services/chat/constraints.txt` like every other install path in this repository.

## Not established

Whether this script is still used, and against which environment. It lives under `infrastructure/scripts/` rather than in the chat service, and nothing in the documented command surface (`make help`, the npm scripts) invokes it. If it is dead, deleting it is a better fix than repairing it — and #151 is the precedent, where a stale script writing into `public/images` was resolved by settling whether it was still anyone's tool.

issue.title: vertexai.generative_models is past its announced removal date, and five chat files import it
issue.body:
Found while verifying #294 (`google-cloud-aiplatform` 1.163.0 -> 1.164.0). Not caused by that bump — the same condition holds at 1.163.0 — but the bump is what put a spotlight on it, and the timing makes it worth acting on rather than filing and forgetting.

## Measured

From the installed package's own `METADATA`, identical in 1.163.0 and 1.164.0:

> The following Generative AI modules in the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform SDK are deprecated as of June 24, 2025 and will be removed on **June 24, 2026**

Today is **2026-08-17**. That removal date passed 54 days ago and the modules are still shipping — verified by importing them under `-W error::DeprecationWarning` on 1.164.0, which raises nothing.

So the deprecation window has expired, the removal has not happened yet, and the changelog carries no further notice. The next release that does remove it is under no obligation to announce it again.

## What breaks when it lands

Five files import the affected surface directly:

```
services/chat/src/api/contoso_chat/chat_request.py
services/chat/src/api/evaluators/custom_evals/coherence.py
services/chat/src/api/evaluators/custom_evals/fluency.py
services/chat/src/api/evaluators/custom_evals/groundedness.py
services/chat/src/api/evaluators/custom_evals/relevance.py
```

`chat_request.py` is the live GCP chat path, not just evaluation tooling.

## Why the usual "CI will catch it" does not reassure here

It will catch the *import*, because `tests/unit/test_evaluators.py` performs a real `import vertexai` and a real `vertexai.init(...)` against the installed package. So a removal produces a red dependabot PR rather than a silent break. That much is fine.

What CI cannot catch is anything subtler, and this is the part worth recording: **nothing in this repository ever makes a real, credentialed `generate_content` call at any version.**

- `tests/unit/test_chat_request.py::test_generate_llm_response_gcp_provider` replaces `sys.modules["vertexai"]` and `sys.modules["vertexai.generative_models"]` with fakes, so it never touches the installed package.
- `tests/unit/test_evaluators.py` does import for real and does call `vertexai.init` for real, but mocks `GenerativeModel` before `generate_content`.
- `make e2e-smoke` never reaches vertexai at all. It raises earlier, at `services/chat/src/api/search_service.py:95` — `PROJECT_ID, REGION, and DISCOVERY_ENGINE_DATASTORE_ID must be set` — before `generate_llm_response` is called. Setting `E2E_REQUIRE_REAL_CHAT=1` does not help; it fails for missing datastore config instead.

That is a standing coverage gap rather than something this bump introduced, but it bounds what any green run can tell you about this dependency: it proves the import surface resolves, and nothing about behaviour.

## Options

1. **Migrate to the Google Gen AI SDK** (`google-genai`), which is what the deprecation notice directs users to. Real work across five files, and it changes the live chat path, so it wants its own slice and its own testing story.
2. **Pin `google-cloud-aiplatform` and stop taking bumps** until the migration is done, so removal cannot arrive unannounced. It is already pinned exactly, so this means a dependabot ignore rule rather than a code change — and it trades a sudden break for a knowingly stale dependency.
3. **Leave it and rely on CI's import-level catch**, having recorded here what the failure will look like and which five files it lands in.

Option 1 is the only one that ends it. Whether it is worth doing now depends on how much the GCP provider path is actually used, which is not established here — `LLM_PROVIDER=local` is the documented local default, and the smoke has never exercised the GCP path for real.

## Not established

- Whether `google-genai` covers everything the four evaluators and `chat_request.py` need, or whether the migration changes behaviour as well as imports.
- Whether the removal is genuinely imminent or whether the date has quietly slipped. Two months past with no removal suggests slippage, but that is an inference from one observation and this repository has a written history of those being wrong.

# Contoso Outdoors Company Website

A modern e-commerce website for "Contoso Outdoors" with integrated AI features, built with Next.js, Tailwind CSS, and PostgreSQL.

The web application source lives in `apps/web/`, and the chat service lives in `services/chat/`.

## Table of Contents

- [Quick Start](#getting-started)
- [Features](#features)
- [Project Documentation](#project-documentation)
- [Local Development](#option-2-local-development-hybrid)
- [Deployment](#option-3-deploy-to-google-cloud-platform-gcp)
- [Database](#database)
- [Authentication](#authentication)
- [Contributing](#contributing)

## Getting Started

Choose one of the following three options to run the application:

## Toolchain Baseline

Local development and coding-agent workflows are standardized on:

- Node.js `22`
- Python `3.11`

This repo uses `mise` for local runtime pinning:

```bash
mise install
```

All Python runs from a project virtualenv at `.venv` (git-ignored). `make bootstrap`
creates it, and every Make target invokes `.venv/bin/python` directly — there is
nothing to activate. To create it on its own:

```bash
make venv
```

### Option 1: Run Everything Locally (Docker)
**Best for:** Trying out the application quickly without installing dependencies.

This runs the Web App, AI Chat Service, and Database in containers. The default chat image uses a lightweight dependency profile for faster CI and local startup.

1.  **Clone the repository:**
    ```bash
    git clone https://github.com/your-username/contoso.git
    cd contoso
    ```

2.  **(Optional) Prepare Local AI:**
    - Install [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) and run `ollama pull gemma3:12b`.

3.  **Create `.env`:**
    ```bash
    cp .env.example .env
    ```
    Then edit values as needed for your environment.

4.  **Start:**
    ```bash
    docker-compose up
    ```
    - Web App: [http://localhost:3100](http://localhost:3100)
    - Chat Service: [http://localhost:8100](http://localhost:8100)

### Option 2: Local Development (Hybrid)
**Best for:** developing the Next.js application with hot-reloading.

> **Updating existing env files.** The published host ports moved off the
> contended defaults — web `3100`, chat `8100`, database `55432`. Neither
> `.env` nor `services/chat/.env` is tracked, so older ones still name `3000`,
> `8000` and `5432`, and every one of those fails by *reaching something else*
> rather than by erroring: `CHAT_ENDPOINT` posts your `CHAT_API_KEY` to
> whatever now owns the old port, and the chat service's `DATABASE_URL` runs
> raw SQL against whatever owns `5432`.
>
> Re-copy both from their `.env.example`, or update `NEXTAUTH_URL`,
> `CHAT_ENDPOINT`, `DATABASE_URL` and `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` by hand.
> `make agent-doctor` names every drifted key, and `make bootstrap` runs it —
> worth one of the two if you set this up before the ports moved.


1.  **Start Database & Chat Service:**
    ```bash
    docker-compose up -d db chat
    ```

2.  **Configure `.env`:**
    ```bash
    cp .env.example .env
    ```
    Then edit values as needed for your environment.

3.  **Run Migrations:**
    ```bash
    make migrate-deploy
    ```
    This applies the migrations already in `apps/web/prisma/migrations/`. Use
    `make migrate NAME=<migration-name>` only when you have changed
    `schema.prisma` and want to author a new one.

4.  **Start Web App:**
    ```bash
    make dev-web
    ```
    or
    ```bash
    npm run dev:web
    ```
    - Web App: [http://localhost:3100](http://localhost:3100)

    The dev server uses the same 3100 the composed `web` service publishes, so
    `NEXTAUTH_URL` in `.env` is correct for both options. Running this *and*
    the full `docker-compose up` at once is the one case where they collide —
    Option 2 expects only `db` and `chat` in Docker.

For a fresh Docker DB volume (schema + seed + chat reindex) use:

```bash
make docker-init-fresh
```

### Option 3: Deploy to Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
**Best for:** Production deployment with Vertex AI.

1.  **Prerequisites:** Google Cloud SDK, Docker, Terraform, Billing Account.

2.  **Environment:**
    ```bash
    export PROJECT_ID="your-project-id"
    export BILLING_ACCOUNT="your-billing-id"
    export NEXTAUTH_SECRET="your-secret"
    ```

3.  **Deploy:**
    ```bash
    ./infrastructure/scripts/setup_project.sh
    ```
    This script provisions Cloud SQL, Cloud Run, and deploys the entire stack.

---

## Common Commands

The repository now includes a root `Makefile` for a consistent command surface:

```bash
make help
make bootstrap
make venv
make toolchain-doctor
make env-contract-check
make agent-doctor
make env-init
make setup
make setup-chat-full
make local-provider-check
make diagnose-chat-local
make docker-init-fresh
make dev
make test
make test-scripts
make quick-ci
make quick-ci-changed
make e2e-smoke
make e2e-smoke-lite
make e2e-smoke-full
make release-dry-run
make ci
```

There is also a root `package.json` workspace command surface:

```bash
npm run bootstrap
npm run doctor
npm run env-contract-check
npm run setup
npm run setup:chat:full
npm run local-provider-check
npm run diagnose:chat:local
npm run dev:web
npm run dev:chat
npm run test:scripts
npm run quick-ci
npm run quick-ci:changed
npm run quick-ci:chat
npm run e2e:smoke
npm run e2e:smoke:lite
npm run e2e:smoke:full
npm run release:dry-run
npm run ci:web
npm run ci:chat
npm run ci
```

## Chat Dependency Profiles

- `core` (default): fastest local/CI path, no local LLM/vector libraries.
- `full`: includes local LLM/vector libraries (`torch`, `litellm`, `chromadb`, `sentence-transformers`).

Use `core` for normal CI and contract checks:

```bash
make setup-chat
make e2e-smoke-lite
```

Use `full` when validating `LLM_PROVIDER=local` behavior:

```bash
make setup-chat-full
make e2e-smoke-full
ollama serve
ollama pull gemma3:12b
```

import asyncio
import json

import jsonlines
import pandas as pd
from contoso_chat.chat_request import get_response
from evaluators.custom_evals.coherence import coherence_evaluation
from evaluators.custom_evals.fluency import fluency_evaluation
from evaluators.custom_evals.groundedness import groundedness_evaluation
from evaluators.custom_evals.relevance import relevance_evaluation
from prompty.tracer import trace
from tracing import init_tracing

# %% [markdown]
# ## Get output from data and save to results jsonl file

# %%
@trace
def load_data():
    data_path = "./evaluators/data.jsonl"

    df = pd.read_json(data_path, lines=True)
    df.head()
    return df

# %%
async def create_response_data_async(df):
    results = []

    for _, row in df.iterrows():
        customer_id = row["customerId"]
        question = row["question"]

        # Run contoso-chat/chat_request flow to get response.
        response = await get_response(customer_id=customer_id, question=question, chat_history=[])
        print(response)

        # Add results to list.
        result = {
            "question": question,
            "context": response["context"],
            "answer": response["answer"],
        }
        results.append(result)

    # Save results to a JSONL file.
    with open("result.jsonl", "w") as file:
        for result in results:
            file.write(json.dumps(result) + "\n")
    return results


@trace
def create_response_data(df):
    return asyncio.run(create_response_data_async(df))

# %%
@trace
def evaluate():
    # Evaluate results from results file
    results_path = 'result.jsonl'
    results = []
    with open(results_path, 'r') as file:
        for line in file:
            print(line)
            results.append(json.loads(line))

    for result in results:
        question = result['question']
        context = result['context']
        answer = result['answer']
        
        groundedness_score = groundedness_evaluation(question=question, answer=answer, context=context)
        fluency_score = fluency_evaluation(question=question, answer=answer, context=context)
        coherence_score = coherence_evaluation(question=question, answer=answer, context=context)
        relevance_score = relevance_evaluation(question=question, answer=answer, context=context)
        
        result['groundedness'] = groundedness_score
        result['fluency'] = fluency_score
        result['coherence'] = coherence_score
        result['relevance'] = relevance_score

    # Save results to a JSONL file
    with open('result_evaluated.jsonl', 'w') as file:
        for result in results:
            file.write(json.dumps(result) + '\n')

    with jsonlines.open('eval_results.jsonl', 'w') as writer:
        writer.write(results)
    # Print results

    df = pd.read_json('result_evaluated.jsonl', lines=True)
    df.head()
    
    return df

# %%
@trace
def create_summary(df):
    print("Evaluation summary:\n")
    print(df)
    # drop question, context and answer
    mean_df = df.drop(["question", "context", "answer"], axis=1).mean()
    print("\nAverage scores:")
    print(mean_df)
    df.to_markdown('eval_results.md')
    with open('eval_results.md', 'a') as file:
        file.write("\n\nAverages scores:\n\n")
    mean_df.to_markdown('eval_results.md', 'a')

    print("Results saved to result_evaluated.jsonl")

# %%
# create main funciton for python script
if __name__ == "__main__":
   tracer = init_tracing(local_tracing=True)
   test_data_df = load_data()
   response_results = create_response_data(test_data_df)
   result_evaluated = evaluate()
   create_summary(result_evaluated)

"""
Master script to seed all data into Google Cloud Platform.
This script orchestrates the seeding of both products and customers.
